text.title: ember benchmark report
text.subtitle: Calibrated advice for coding agents from Cloudflare's Clef-Flash, measured on the five decision recipes of ember's agent kit
context: ember runs Cloudflare's Clef-Flash decision model [@clef] locally on Apple Silicon and gives coding agents one [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) tool, `advise` [@mcp]. An agent sends a `state` (the evidence) and a set of typed questions, and ember returns a probability for every option of every question. It generates no text: it advises, and the agent decides.

Clef is a decision model, not a chat model. A Qwen3.5 backbone with a joint schema head scores the options of every question in one forward pass, so the questions in one call are weighed jointly. ember serves it in fp16 on the Apple GPU (MPS) behind a local HTTP server.

Agents act on ember's answers through thresholds published in ember's agent kit: trust a `choice` at confidence 0.85 or above, read a `noul` as yes at P >= 0.80 and no at P <= 0.20, and read a `score` through its expected value. A threshold is only safe when confidence tracks accuracy, so this benchmark measures calibration and the outcomes of those decision rules, not only accuracy.

question_types.returns: The top option, its confidence, and the full distribution
question_types.correct: The top option is the gold option

question_types.returns: A distribution over levels and its expected value
question_types.correct: The expected value rounds to the gold level

system: Two runners exercise the same server. The benchmark runner posts every item to the model server's `POST /v1/systemone`, the endpoint the MCP tool forwards to, so it measures the model and server end to end. The agent eval runner drives a real coding agent through `opencode run --pure`, so it also measures whether the agent calls ember at the right moments, asks well, and acts on the answer.

dataset: The dataset has 58 items and 644 scored questions: 0 `choice`, 644 `noul`, and 0 `score`. Each line is self-contained: the `state`, the recipe's fixed question set, a gold label for every question, its source, and a one-line rationale. Other implementations can score it without this harness.

0 items reproduce the worked examples in the agent kit's playbook and sit in `dev`; the other 58 were written for this benchmark. Items are split into `dev` (27 items, for tuning) and `test` (31 items, for reporting), stratified so that every label of every question appears in both. The dataset card below answers the datasheet questions of [@gebru2021].
protocol: Labels were judged from `state` and the option descriptions alone, and were fixed before any model run. *(since dataset version `1e1bb88d47f0`)*
`needs_review` is true exactly when `risk` is Medium or High, and `retry` is true only for `flaky` failures. *(since dataset version `1e1bb88d47f0`)*
Drafts whose evidence fit two options were rewritten or dropped while authoring, before any run. *(since dataset version `1e1bb88d47f0`)*

A label changes only when a reviewer finds it wrong on its merits, never because the model disagreed. A change to any item's state, media, questions, gold, or split alters the dataset's content hash, which each run records, so runs on different label sets cannot be compared by accident; annotations (kind, tier, source, rationale) do not. *(since dataset version `1e1bb88d47f0`)*

Every `score` scale runs from least to most of the quantity its instruction names; index 0 is always the least. The expected score is read in those units. A scale is never reversed to make a label read naturally. *(since dataset version `1e1bb88d47f0`)*

For a `noul` question, P(true) is the probability of the condition the instruction names; the condition is phrased so that `true` is the pole that calls for caution. *(since dataset version `1e1bb88d47f0`)*
datasheet: To measure whether ember's probabilities are accurate and calibrated enough for agents to act on the agent kit's thresholds, and to compare model revisions and setups.
58 items across five recipes, 644 scored questions, a gold label per question, a rationale per item.
0 items reproduce the agent kit's worked examples; 58 were written by the ember authors. No user data.
From `state` and the option descriptions alone, fixed before any run, under the rules in the labelling protocol.
Tune on `dev`, report on `test`. It is not a measure of agent behaviour, and not a training set.
Relabelling happens only on review, changes the dataset's SHA-256, and invalidates comparisons with earlier runs.

metrics.name: Accuracy and 95% interval
metrics.definition: The share of scored questions answered correctly. The interval is a percentile bootstrap over questions: 1,000 resamples with replacement (seed 0), reporting the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles [@efron1993].

metrics.name: Macro-F1
metrics.text: F1_c = 2TP_c / (2TP_c + FP_c + FN_c); Macro-F1 = mean over classes
metrics.definition: The unweighted mean of per-class F1, so rare options count as much as common ones; computed as the arithmetic mean of per-class scores [@opitz2019].

metrics.name: Expected and maximum calibration error
metrics.text: ECE = sum_b (n_b / N) * |acc(b) - conf(b)|; MCE = max_b |acc(b) - conf(b)|
metrics.definition: Answers are binned by top-label confidence into B = 10 equal-width bins; ECE is the count-weighted gap between each bin's accuracy and its mean confidence [@naeini2015] [@guo2017]. A `noul` answer's top-label confidence is max(P, 1 - P). With bins of a few items the estimate is noisy and depends on binning [@nixon2019], so read it with the reliability diagrams.

metrics.name: Brier score
metrics.definition: The squared error between the predicted distribution and the one-hot gold label, a proper scoring rule that rewards both calibration and sharpness [@brier1950]. 0 is perfect; the worst is 2 for `choice` and 1 for `noul` (where K = 2 is folded into P(true)).

metrics.name: Ranked probability score
metrics.definition: The proper scoring rule for ordered levels: it compares cumulative distributions, so a near miss costs less than a far one [@epstein1969]. 0 is perfect and 1 the worst.

metrics.name: Mean absolute error
metrics.definition: How far the expected score lands from the gold level. Exact-level accuracy is strict for ordinal judgments, so read it with MAE, RPS, and the share within one level.

metrics.name: Coverage and accuracy at a threshold
metrics.text: coverage(t) = share of answers with confidence >= t; accuracy(t) = accuracy of those answers
metrics.definition: Selective prediction [@geifman2017]: how often an answer clears the threshold at which the kit tells an agent to act, and how accurate those answers are. The curve sweeps the threshold; the markers are the kit's published values.

policies: The agent kit's AGENTS.md snippet ships a default project policy. The report replays it on every item and counts what an agent following it to the letter would have done: the right thing, a cautious extra step (an unnecessary question or review), or a wrong action (acting on a vague request, or shipping a risky change unreviewed).
reliability: A reliability diagram plots each confidence bin's accuracy against its mean confidence; a perfectly calibrated advisor sits on the diagonal [@degroot1983]. Bars above the diagonal mean ember was more often right than its confidence claimed (under-confidence); bars below it mean over-confidence, the dangerous direction for threshold-driven agents.
limitations: **Sample size.** 644 questions give a 95% interval about 6 points wide overall; per-question samples of 20 to 28 are wider still, and calibration bins hold a few items each.

**Single rater.** One maintainer labels every item from `state` and the option descriptions; no inter-rater figure exists and none is shown. The blinded re-labelling that publishes label stability (an optimistic bound on the human ceiling) is pending (Phase 1). Shared assumptions could make items easier or harder for ember than real traffic.
**Curated, not sampled.** Items are short, English, and written for the benchmark rather than drawn from real agent sessions.
**Ordinal judgments.** Risk and effort levels are judgments; neighbouring levels are often defensible, which is why MAE, RPS, and within-one are reported alongside exact accuracy.
**One model, one machine.** One pinned model revision in fp16 on MPS; numerics on CPU or CUDA can differ slightly. Repeat runs on the same server are deterministic for identical requests.
**Fixed question sets.** Questions are weighed jointly, so results hold for these question sets. The routing and effort option sets are templates; a project that replaces them should measure its own.
**Model and server only.** The benchmark calls the HTTP endpoint directly. It does not measure an agent's decision to consult ember or the quality of the questions it writes.
reproduce: make bootstrap               # dependencies, pinned weights, readiness check
ember start                  # warm model server on 127.0.0.1:8765
ember eval run               # every item; or --split test, --category <recipe>
ember eval export            # this report: Markdown, HTML, figures, raw data
glossary: The evidence an agent passes to ember: a string or JSON object.
A fixed question set for one kind of decision, from the agent kit.
A yes/no question; the answer is P(true).
A question over named options; the answer is a distribution.
A question over ordered levels; the answer is a distribution and its expected value.
The probability of the answer's chosen option, or max(P, 1 - P) for a noul.
The share of answers that clear a decision threshold.
A decision rule from the agent kit, such as 'stop for review when needs_review >= 0.80 or risk >= 2.0'.

findings.title: Overall accuracy
findings.text: 80.1% of 644 questions were answered correctly (95% CI 77.2% to 83.1%), and 5.2% of 58 items had every question right.

findings.title: Answers past the kit's thresholds
findings.text: 433 of 485 answers that cleared the kit's act-on-it thresholds (choice confidence >= 0.85; noul P >= 0.80 or <= 0.20) were correct (89.3%).

findings.title: noul calibration
findings.text: noul answers are over-confident: mean top-label confidence 0.87 against 80.1% accuracy (ECE 0.070).

findings.title: Strongest and weakest questions
findings.text: concept/diegetic is strongest at 100.0%; status/draft is weakest at 0.0%.

findings.title: dev and test agree
findings.text: dev scored 79.5% and test 80.6%; their 95% intervals overlap.

Tools — mcpvault

The `@bitbonsai/mcpvault` MCP server provides agents with filesystem-based read/write access to the vault at `docs/vault/`, without requiring an Obsidian instance to be running. Configured via `opencode.json` at the repository root; invoked automatically by OpenCode at session start.

## Entry Point

```
npx -y @bitbonsai/mcpvault@0.11.0 {vault_absolute_path}
```

## Inputs

- Absolute filesystem path to `docs/vault/`
- MCP tool calls from the connected agent (via `opencode.json` MCP config block)

## Outputs

- Note content (read operations: `read_note`, `read_multiple_notes`, `search_notes`)
- Write confirmations (write/append: `write_note`, `append_to_note`, `patch_note`)
- Frontmatter updates (AST-aware: `update_frontmatter`, `manage_tags`)
- Vault structure (list: `list_vault`, `list_all_tags`)

## Dependencies

- Node.js ≥ 18.0.0 (invoked via `npx`; no global install required)
- `@bitbonsai/mcpvault` v0.11.0 (pinned; latest available as of 2026-04-21)

## Configuration

Configured in `opencode.json` at the repository root (project-local; additive relative to Concourse global config):

```json
{
  "mcp": {
    "obsidian": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": ["npx", "-y", "@bitbonsai/mcpvault@0.11.0", "/path/to/docs/vault"],
      "enabled": true
    }
  }
}
```

This does NOT interact with `.concourse.json` (Concourse's repo-profile hook for github/gdai-mcp-server/gdscript) — the two files serve different systems and are independent.

Does NOT ship in the game binary. Dev-time only.

## Key Tool Surface (15 tools)

| Tool | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `read_note` | Read single note by path |
| `search_notes` | BM25 full-text search with frontmatter filters |
| `write_note` | Create note with YAML validation |
| `append_to_note` | Append content (backlinks, session logs) |
| `list_vault` | Enumerate vault files (orphan-check) |
| `update_frontmatter` | AST-aware field update (no field corruption) |
| `read_multiple_notes` | Batch read for context injection |
| `list_all_tags` | Enumerate all tags in vault |
| `manage_tags` | Add/remove tags without overwriting frontmatter |
| `patch_note` | Surgical section replacement |
| soft-delete | `trashMode` parameter — never use on session logs |

See `docs/vault/Specs/080 Agent Vault Knowledge Graph/contracts/mcp-tools.md` for the full tool surface contract.

## Agent Write Protocol

Agents MUST follow the write-back protocol in AGENTS.md (Vault Knowledge Graph section) before calling `write_note`. Key rules:

- All 9 required frontmatter fields must be populated before writing
- `related:` must contain ≥1 link resolving to a hub note in `Systems/`, `Design/`, or `Governance/`
- No inline code excerpts in note bodies
- Notes start at `status: draft`; agents may self-promote to `reviewed` (same session)

## MCP Selection Rationale

Selected over `revanp/obsidian-md-mcp` (disqualified: 6 tools, `write_note` passes raw strings with no frontmatter preservation — silent corruption risk). See `docs/vault/Specs/080 Agent Vault Knowledge Graph/research.md` R-001.

## Related

- [[Tools — Agent Skills & MCP]] — broader inventory of OpenCode skills and all MCP servers (mcpvault is one of four)
- [[Tools — Vault Audit]] — mechanical and semantic audit pipeline that complements the MCP write protocol
- [[Tools — Development Workbench]] — meta-architecture showing how mcpvault fits with personas, agents, and CI

Horror Register

The operational vocabulary for evaluating whether a design choice, visual asset, sound, or interaction belongs in Old Growth. The Horror Register defines what is *in* and what is *out* — used as a filter at every phase of production.

This note is the checklist companion to [[Design/Tone and Horror]], which contains the full philosophical grounding, three horror pillars, and film lineage. Read that note first.

## In Register

These are valid in Old Growth:

- **Dread before revelation** — the feeling of wrongness before anything has happened
- **Environmental hostility** — the forest registers the player's presence; it does not react, it accumulates
- **Material horror** — biological, geological, ancient; never supernatural in the conventional sense
- **Indifference** — the threat does not want the player dead; it does not want anything
- **Wrong-but-almost-natural** — anomalies that are uncanny, not impossible; disturbing because they *almost* fit
- **Sanctuary contrast** — the bus is safe, the outside is not; this contrast is load-bearing
- **Diegetic unease** — all feedback through the world itself (dashboard, audio, road feel); no HUD screaming
- **Accumulation** — disturbance, contamination, degradation build across time without announcement
- **Scale** — the forest is older than roads; the player's presence is trivially small

## Out of Register

These break the tone and must be avoided:

- **Jump scares as primary tool** — habituate within minutes; structural horror does not rely on them
- **Legible monster** — anything with a personality, a motive, or legible anger becomes manageable
- **Gore-as-shock** — visceral imagery deployed for disgust or instant reaction is out of register; biological horror that is *wrong-beautiful* (contamination, calcification, spore film) is within the "Flesh as Horror" pillar and is valid
- **Narrative exposition** — the forest is never explained; characters do not describe what it is
- **Defeat** — the condition cannot be mastered; any design implying "beat the forest" breaks the thesis
- **Cartoon or anime aesthetic** — visual direction is painterly Pacific Northwest, editorial documentary
- **Comedy or irony** — the game takes itself seriously; no winking at the player
- **Combat as solution** — on foot the player has no tools that change outcomes; a thrown rock is noise displaced elsewhere, a flare redirects attention, found firearms are empty or corroded; any mechanic implying the condition can be fought breaks the thesis

## Application

When evaluating a new feature, asset, or interaction:

1. Does it reinforce dread or does it release tension prematurely?
2. Does it make the threat feel more indifferent or more intentional?
3. Does it make the bus feel safer or erode sanctuary?
4. Does it fit the "wrong-but-almost-natural" uncanny register?

If a design choice fails two or more of these, reconsider before implementing.

## Related

- [[Design/Tone and Horror]] — the full horror taxonomy, three pillars, film lineage, directorial discipline
- [[Design/Core Mechanics]] — how horror register maps to mechanical design
- [[Systems/Disturbance]] — the primary accumulation mechanic
- [[The Disturbance Thread]] — how the mechanics express the horror

Tech Stack Review

The technology stack decisions for Old Growth — what was chosen, what was evaluated and rejected, and where the open risks are. The authoritative approved stack lives in constitution Appendix A; this note captures the *why* behind each decision.

## Overview

Old Growth's stack is deliberately conservative where possible and opinionated where necessary. The engine and scripting language are locked by constitution (Article III). Vehicle physics, terrain, procedural generation, and audio are locked with strong alternative-assessment. A handful of visual effects and content questions remain open.

**Status legend:**
- 🟢 **Locked** — researched, tested compatibility, no meaningful alternative
- 🟡 **Strong lean** — best option found but alternatives exist worth discussing
- 🟠 **Open** — decision made but could reasonably go another way
- 🔴 **Unresolved** — no decision yet or significant uncertainty

## Key Decisions — Core Stack (all 🟢)

| System | Pick | Why |
|--------|------|-----|
| Game engine | Godot 4.6+ | Native Metal renderer, plaintext GDScript (agent-readable), MIT, Jolt built-in, strong macOS export |
| Scripting | GDScript + Rust (gdext) | GDScript for scene glue; Rust for performance-critical (Article III Rule 17) |
| Physics | Jolt (native in 4.6+) | More stable vehicle sim than Godot Physics; GEVP-compatible |
| Target platform | macOS Universal Binary | Scope constraint; Apple Silicon (Metal) + Intel Macs |
| Physics tick | 120 Hz | GEVP requires 120+; 60 causes instability; 240 is unnecessary |

## Vehicle Physics

- **Vehicle controller**: GEVP (vendored in `addons/`, MIT). Raycast-based, keyboard-friendly, single-script, simcade preset. Needs tuning for 1963 VW Samba feel (rear-engine RWD, ~1100 kg, ~50 HP, high CoG, soft suspension, long braking distances).
- **Engine audio**: Pitch-scaled `AudioStreamPlayer3D` loops (🟠). Simplest approach; may upgrade to multi-sample crossfade in audio polish.

## Terrain & Roads

- **Terrain system**: Terrain3D (C++ GDExtension, MIT). GPU clipmap, foliage instancer, 32 textures, Road Generator connector.
- **Road generation**: Godot Road Generator (🟡). Designed for hand-placed roads; procedural usage is supported but less documented. **Technical risk for spec 053 remediation.**
- **Foliage**: Terrain3D built-in instancer (🟡). Must handle biome-specific vegetation swaps.
- **Heightmap**: FastNoiseLite (Godot built-in). Sufficient for ~2km² worlds.

## Weather & Atmosphere

- Rain-on-Glass shader (🟡), custom wiper integration (🟠)
- Volumetric fog: Godot 4 built-in (🟢)
- Sky: ProceduralSkyMaterial (🟡) — must produce three distinct biome sky feels
- Weather zones: Voronoi/grid subdivision (🟡, novel system)

## Visual Effects & Post-Processing

- Post-processing: ArseniyMirniy Color Correction (🟢, vendored)
- Windshield crack overlay (🟠), Storm wall shader (🟠), biome transition blending (🟡)

## Anomaly Systems

Most anomalies use standard Godot primitives (AnimationPlayer, Area3D, GPUParticles3D, OmniLight3D, MeshInstance3D). See [[Anomalies]] for design specifications; tech choices here are typically 🟢 Locked.

## Audio

- **Audio management**: Godot native (🟢). Sound Manager (nathanhoad) evaluated and rejected (insufficient — no AudioStreamPlayer3D, no AudioEffect manipulation, ambient pool limited to 1 stream).
- **Bus architecture**: 7 buses planned per constitution Appendix A (Master → Ambience, Proximity, Interior, Horror, Radio, RadioDegraded). Currently only Master + Radio + RadioDegraded exist in `src/default_bus_layout.tres`; the remaining buses are being built incrementally through the audio specs. See [[Audio — Overview]] for the CONFLICT callout and [[Conflicts]] for the indexed entry.
- **Positional**: `AudioStreamPlayer3D` built-in (🟢)

## On-Foot Systems

- CharacterBody3D + custom FPS controller (🟡)
- Car entry/exit: custom camera reparent + input context switch (🟠) — **highest-risk custom system**, ~200 lines
- Combat: melee raycast + ranged hitscan/projectile (🟢) — per Article II, on-foot scope is strictly bounded
- Enemy AI: StateMachine + NavigationAgent3D (🟡) — **must verify NavMesh bakes on Terrain3D at runtime**

## Disturbance & Storm

- Disturbance meter: autoload with add(amount, source) + threshold signals (🟢, matches Article X)
- Disturbance HUD: organic visual indicator (🟠, creative risk)
- Storm wall direction: spawn opposite nearest exit, advance toward player (🟢)

## Persistence & Architecture

- **Save**: Godot Resource serialization (`.tres`) (🟡). World state NOT saved — only garage/player state (Article IV Rule 6).
- **Settings**: `ConfigFile` at `user://settings.cfg` (🟢)
- **Cross-system communication**: Signal bus autoload (`events.gd`) (🟢, Article VI)
- **Game state**: `GameState` autoload + enum states (🟡)

## Assets & Pipeline

- **3D format**: glTF 2.0 (.glb) (🟢)
- **VW Samba model**: Placeholder (Kenney) → custom/purchased (🟠). No perfect free 1963 VW Type 2 Samba (23-window, V-nose, two-tone, curved skylight).
- **PBR textures**: CC0 (ambientCG, cgbookcase, Polyhaven) (🟢)
- **Audio assets**: CC0 (Freesound, OpenGameArt, Kenney) (🟡) — fungal/stone SFX may need original recording
- **Radio music**: 🔴 UNRESOLVED. Need 30+ min across multiple genres. CC0 music is rare; AI-generated is an option; doesn't block until audio polish phase.

## macOS Packaging

- Code signing: Apple Developer ID ($99/yr) or ad-hoc (🟠)
- Distribution: DMG with drag-to-Applications (🟢)
- Game controller: Godot GameController built-in (🟢)

## Highest-Risk Open Questions

The source doc identifies six items as the highest technical risks:

1. **Procedural road algorithm** — connected road network from a seed over ~2km² (spec 053)
2. **NavMesh on Terrain3D** — does NavigationAgent3D bake reliably? If not, fall back to raycast steering.
3. **Biome texture swap in Terrain3D** — texture-set-per-region capability
4. **World generation performance** — ~2km² world in <5 seconds on M4 Max (Article V)
5. **Petrified Zone screen-space shader** — selective desaturation of meshes in a 3D area without affecting HUD
6. **Storm wall directional shader** — dramatic shader for an advancing flat plane

## Summary Counts (per source)

- **🟢 Locked**: 26 decisions
- **🟡 Strong lean**: 15 decisions
- **🟠 Open**: 8 decisions
- **🔴 Unresolved**: 1 decision (radio music content)

- [[Build System]] — the CI pipeline that enforces these choices

NoiseHelper Utility Class Design

This note records the structural decisions made for noise_helper.gd during spec 081 (Code Dedup Consolidation) that are non-obvious from the code alone.

## No extends, No class_name

noise_helper.gd declares neither extends nor class_name. It is accessed exclusively via a preload constant in each consuming file:

    const NoiseHelper = preload("res://scripts/generation/noise_helper.gd")

This pattern was chosen over class_name for two reasons. First, the class_name restriction from the constitution applies to autoloads because of Godot 4.6 singleton name conflicts — noise_helper.gd is not an autoload, so class_name would technically be valid. However, making it a named class creates a global symbol that pollutes the project namespace for what is a narrow utility. Preload constants keep the dependency explicit and local. Second, unlike OGTestBase (which uses class_name intentionally so test files can extend it by name), noise_helper.gd has no inheritance use case — callers call its static factory methods, they do not extend it.

## Dictionary Parameter Convention

The create_roughness_noise factory method accepts all parameters via a Dictionary rather than positional arguments. This means every caller must pass their own @export values explicitly:

    NoiseHelper.create_roughness_noise({"octaves": octaves, "frequency": frequency, ...})

No default values are baked into the helper. This was intentional: the helper exists to eliminate duplicate noise setup code, not to encode defaults. If defaults lived inside the helper, callers that relied on them would become silently coupled to the helper's internal values rather than to their own @export variables. The Dictionary convention keeps designer-tunable parameters visible in the caller's inspector.

## References

- src/scripts/generation/noise_helper.gd
- src/scripts/generation/terrain_generator.gd (consumer)
- src/scripts/generation/heightmap_proxy.gd (consumer)
- docs/vault/Sessions/Spec 081 Implementation Session.md

Disturbance System

The disturbance meter is Old Growth's central tension engine. It is not a health bar, not a resource gauge — it is a hidden 0–100 metric that measures how much the forest notices the player. This note captures the design intent AND the full mechanical specification (biological states, disturbance costs, diegetic indicators, Storm behavior). Implementation: [[Autoloads — Disturbance]].

## Overview

The forest does not have a temper. It has a metabolism.

Everything in the woods is input to a process that runs continuously and has been running since before the first road was cut through this watershed. The player's presence feeds this process from the moment they enter the tree line. Every action — collection, combustion, impact, noise — is an input the forest attends to, and attendance accelerates the process.

## Design Intent

This is not punishment. A fallen log feeds the same process. The player is simply a more active source. The disturbance system exists to make the **condition visible through its consequences** rather than through a dedicated UI display. The forest does not provide one. It expects you to have been paying attention.

The constitutional basis is Article X — The Disturbance Is the Design:
> The disturbance system is the primary tension engine. Tension MUST be cycled — not held at a constant level. The forest MUST have moments of apparent safety (negative feedback loop releasing) before escalating again.

## Key Decisions

### Meter

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Range | 0 – 100 |
| Display | None. Never shown directly. |
| In-run reset | None. Never resets during a run. |
| Cross-run behavior | Resets to 0 at run start |
| Read mechanism | Bus behavior, condition presence, audio register shifts, instrument reliability |

Players read disturbance state through environmental cues, not through any HUD element.

### Biological States

| State | Meter Range | Bus Behavior | Condition Presence | Audio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Calm | 0–30 | Normal | Ambient, diffuse | Normal biome ambience |
| Uneasy | 30–60 | Instruments drift slightly | Heightened, directional | Ambience shifts register, lower frequencies |
| Agitated | 60–85 | Instruments unreliable, engine hesitant | Dense, attending | Ambience becomes directional, pulse-like |
| Storm | 85–100 | Electrical instability | Maximum concentration | All frequencies collapse inward |

At 85, the Storm spawns regardless of player position. The Storm state does not have a stable ceiling — it triggers immediately.

### Disturbance Costs (complete table)

| Action | Disturbance Added |
|---|---|
| Fuel canister collected | +3 |
| Repair kit collected | +4 |
| Medkit collected | +5 |
| Flashlight battery collected | +3 |
| Flare gun collected | +3 |
| Flare gun fired | +6 |
| Rock thrown | +0.5 |
| Road contact at speed (condition dispersal) | +5 |
| Engine revving (high RPM) | +1 per second |
| Headlights active | +0.2 per second |
| Flashlight active | +0.2 per second |
| Horn | +3 |
| Player sprinting on foot | +0.5 per second |
| Exiting vehicle | +2 |
| Vehicle collision | +2 |
| Mycelium Network contact | +4 |
| Deadfall triggered | +2 |
| Entering Petrifold (first crossing per run) | +3 |
| Entering Fungal Depths (first crossing per run) | +0 — transition is passive |

### Diegetic Disturbance Indicators

No HUD. Players learn to read:

- **Bus instruments**: drift and jitter increase with disturbance state. At Agitated, instruments become unreliable.
- **Engine audio**: hesitation and irregularity at Agitated. Instability at Storm.
- **Ambient audio**: low-frequency content increases. The forest gets quieter in the wrong way. The sense of being attended-to increases, though this cannot be instrumented.
- **Radio**: signal degradation is driven by both biome depth AND disturbance. Heavy static in Verdant indicates Uneasy or higher. In Fungal Depths, signal degradation is biome-baseline regardless of disturbance — its absence there is not a reliable disturbance indicator.
- **Windshield accumulation**: particulate and biological matter accumulate faster at higher disturbance.
- **Perception**: at high disturbance AND high exposure, familiar routes feel different. Whether this is the condition or the player is not distinguishable by any available instrument.

### Tension-Release Cycles (Article X Rule)

Tension MUST be cycled — not held at a constant level. The forest MUST have moments of apparent safety (negative feedback loop releasing) before escalating again. Per Article XII-J: a horror experience that never releases becomes numbing within minutes.

Within a run, the meter can only climb — but the *experienced* tension releases when the player finds moments of momentum (driving cleanly, avoiding a Deadfall), audio pockets of quiet (between anomaly zones), or successful on-foot collection. The metabolism continues; the player's felt-state relaxes briefly before the next climb.

### Biome-Reactive Response

Each [[Biomes|biome]] has a distinct disturbance response profile (see [[Biome Behavior]] concept thread). The same player action may feed the process differently in Fungal Depths than in Verdant Old Growth. The audio arc, radio degradation curve, and anomaly expression all vary per biome even for the same disturbance level.

### The Storm (Finishing State)

The Storm spawns when the disturbance meter reaches 85. It cannot be cancelled or reversed after spawning.

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Trigger threshold | 85 disturbance |
| Spawn location | Crater rim, opposite side from nearest exit corridor (terraforming energy radiates inward from the reshape boundary) |
| Initial speed | 20 km/h |
| Speed acceleration | +5 km/h per 20 seconds |
| Maximum speed | 80 km/h (reached at ~4 minutes) |
| Width | Full crater width — no flanking |
| Player damage inside | 30 HP/sec |
| Van damage inside | 15 HP/sec |
| Tree behavior in path | Incorporated (visual effect, not obstacle) |
| Audio pre-visualization | Subsonic rumble → ambience collapse → silence → Storm |

**Survival window**: from spawn, the player has a meaningful survival window if already near an exit. The window narrows based on distance from exit and current speed. A player at the far end of the map must drive hard and without detours to extract.

The Storm is not avoidable through off-road detours — it spans the full crater width. The only variable is speed toward an exit corridor.

If the player is caught and survives the initial damage (possible at full health), the bus will be destroyed within seconds. On-foot survival inside the Storm is not possible.

### Designer-Tunable

Per Article VI Rule 3 / Article XII-J: tension-release cycles MUST be tunable via `@export` variables. Thresholds for Ambient → Directed → Cascade → Finishing (implemented as Calm → Uneasy → Agitated → Storm) are exposed for design iteration. Config lives in `res://resources/config/disturbance_config.tres` per spec 078.

### Irreversibility

The process never resets during a run. Inputs already fed cannot be recalled. The forest does not forget in the way that implies it was paying attention to begin with — it simply continues, and what has already entered the system has already changed the system.

Across runs, the condition accumulates via the garage contamination axis (see [[World Model]] / [[Narrative Direction]]) — a persistent value the player has no direct way to read but which progressively changes the garage and the bus.

## How It Appears In-Game

The player does not see a number. They see (and hear) consequences:

- Audio degrades on the radio; the bus sounds change
- Anomalies intensify
- Weather worsens
- What moves in the wood gets closer and less cautious
- Eventually, the Storm spawns from the ridgeline and moves toward the player

The Storm is the disturbance reaching Finishing — see [[The Player Causes the Storm]].

## Related

- [[The Crater]] — the origin event whose dimensional energy the disturbance meter measures
- [[The Temporal Fracture]] — disturbance as temporal destabilization; the Storm as ongoing insertion unfiltered
- [[World Model]] — the world the disturbance operates in
- [[Tone and Horror]] — dread-over-shock framing
- [[Core Mechanics]] — the run loop that drives disturbance accumulation
- [[Autoloads — Disturbance]] — the GDScript + Rust implementation
- [[Audio — Car Radio]] — radio degradation as diegetic disturbance readout
- [[Audio — World Audio]] — four-state ambient audio arc
- [[The Disturbance Thread]] — cross-cutting concept thread
- [[The Player Causes the Storm]] — the endgame manifestation
- [[Constitution]] — Article X is the authoritative source, Article XII-J (horror rhythm)

Implementation Choices and Architecture Decisions

Core architectural rules that apply across all implementation work. These are constitutional constraints (Article I, III), not decisions made during any single session.

## Core Architectural Rules

### 1. Signal-Driven Architecture

- **Rule**: All cross-system communication via the `Events` autoload signal bus only. Systems must not call methods on nodes they do not own.
- **Source**: Constitution Article I / `Governance/Constitution.md`
- **Enforcement**: `gdlint` catches direct node references across system boundaries; code review.

### 2. Seeded Randomness

- **Rule**: All procedural systems use `RandomNumberGenerator` seeded from `GameState.current_seed`. Never use global `randf()` / `randi()`.
- **Source**: Constitution Article III Rule 4
- **Enforcement**: SC-001 baseline (seed=1250827250 → trees=1452, ferns=5300, logs=3061; post-spec-103 per-tree-clearance, 2026-04-26 per AGENTS.md); `make test` headless run.

### 3. Asset Export Safety

- **Rule**: Non-shippable directories under `src/assets/` must contain a `.gdignore` file. The shippable allowlist lives in `scripts/ci/check_asset_gdignore.sh`.
- **Source**: AGENTS.md § Asset Export Safety; `Discoveries/Asset Export Safety — gdignore.md`
- **Enforcement**: `make gdignore-check` (CI-gated).

### 4. Component SemVer

- **Rule**: Every file under `src/` maps to a component in `src/component_versions.json`. Modifying any file in a component's path requires bumping that component's version.
- **Source**: Constitution Article III Rule 15; `Governance/Component SemVer Policy.md`
- **Enforcement**: `make semver` (CI-gated).

Controls

The control scheme for Old Growth: driving, on-foot, radio, vehicle systems, and debug. Controls are designed to stay out of the way — everything is a simple keyboard action directly mapped to a diegetic interaction with the Samba or the forest.

## Overview

Old Growth uses keyboard+mouse. All controls are direct: no chord inputs, no menus-within-menus, no modifier keys. The cabin view is the HUD; interactions surface when the player looks at the relevant object (radio, dome light).

## Design Intent

Input design serves diegesis (Article XII-G). Looking at the radio to activate its controls is the rule, not the exception — the player interacts with *the thing*, not with an abstraction of the thing. The control map is minimal because the game's complexity lives in the world, not in the input bindings.

## Key Decisions

### Driving

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| W | Accelerate |
| S | Brake / Reverse |
| A | Steer left |
| D | Steer right |
| Space | Handbrake |
| Shift | Toggle gear (forward / reverse) |
| Mouse | Look around cabin |
| Esc | Toggle mouse cursor (captured / free) |

### Vehicle Systems

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| H | Toggle headlights |
| L | Toggle high beams |
| J | Cycle wipers (off / slow / fast) |
| E | Toggle dome light (when focused) |

### Radio

Look at the radio on the dashboard to activate controls.

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| E | Toggle radio power |
| T | Tune frequency up |
| Y | Tune frequency down |
| = | Volume up |
| - | Volume down |

### On Foot

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| W/A/S/D | Move |
| Shift | Sprint |
| Ctrl | Crouch |
| E | Interact |
| F | Toggle flashlight |
| G | Enter / exit vehicle |
| Mouse | Look around |

### General

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| R | Restart scene |
| Esc | Toggle mouse cursor |
| F12 | Take screenshot (saved to `~/Pictures/Old Growth/`) |

### Debug (debug builds only)

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| F1 | Toggle debug overlay (game) / preview info overlay (world preview) |
| F3 | Toggle road spine overlay (game and world preview) |

## How It Appears In-Game

Controls are learned by doing. The game does not display a control reference; the player discovers them through the environment (dashboard labels on the Samba, subtle cues in the garage). On-foot movement is quieter than running; the mycelium notices sprinting — this is a control decision with tonal consequences.

## Related

- [[Core Mechanics]] — the run loop that controls drive
- [[Vehicle — Samba]] — the interactions controls invoke
- [[Audio — Car Radio]] — radio controls are diegetic
- [[Design]] — folder MOC

Spec 099 SFX Pipeline Implementation — Apr 25 2026

This session log records the full implementation of spec 099 (SFX Pipeline Expansion), executed in 8 phases across a single work session on 2026-04-25.

## What Was Done

### Phase 1 — Tooling Infrastructure (T001–T011C)
Makefile sfx-generate / sfx-master / sfx-loop-ogg / sfx-oneshot-ogg / sfx-install targets added to tools/tts/Makefile, parameterized by CATEGORY and OUTPUT. Two new CI validation scripts created: tools/tts/validate_sfx_naming.sh and tools/tts/validate_sfx_provenance.sh. The ambient_process.sh script was extended with --gold-dir / --install-dir arguments (backward-compatible with existing ambient-weather-* callers). Two new audio buses added to src/default_bus_layout.tres: VehicleSFX (Compressor + EQ10) and SFX (Reverb + LowPassFilter). AudioBusConfig resource extended with 8 new @export fields. Events.disturbance_level_changed signal added and emitted from both code paths in Disturbance.add(). SfxBusModulator GDScript created and wired into main.tscn.

### Phase 2 — Gold Directory Scaffolding (T012–T021)
90 provenance JSON stubs created across 37 categories (schema 1.3, ElevenLabs generator, PENDING sha256s). All gold/ directories created with .gdignore files. ElevenLabs minimum duration constraint discovered: 0.5s minimum — all stubs with sub-0.5s duration_seconds values were patched before generation.

### Phase 3 — Tier 1 Vehicle SFX + sfx/ Retirement (T022–T032B)
6 Tier 1 assets generated via ElevenLabs SFX V2 and installed: vehicle_engine_idle.ogg (loop), vehicle_wiper_squeak.ogg (oneshot), vehicle_rim_scrape.ogg (loop), vehicle_tire_pop.ogg (oneshot), vehicle_splash_loop.ogg (loop), interaction_toggle_click.ogg (oneshot). Legacy src/assets/audio/sfx/ directory removed (5 files: engine_idle, rim_scrape, splash_loop, tire_pop, wiper_squeak). Code paths updated: tire_damage_driver.gd, samba_bus.tscn (ext_resource paths + DomeLightControl.toggle_sfx). SplashAudio AudioStreamPlayer3D added to SplashController with vehicle_splash_loop.ogg; splash_particles.gd extended to play/stop audio on particle activation state.

A Makefile bug was discovered and fixed: sfx-generate was incorrectly passing --output with the full path and .wav extension instead of just the basename. This caused the provenance JSON lookup to fail with "not found: vehicle_engine_idle.wav.json".

### Phase 4 — Structure Break SFX + Lightning Wiring (T033–T040)
3 Tier 2 world/anomalies break assets generated: world_prop_break.ogg, world_guardrail_break.ogg, world_power_pole_fall.ogg. BreakAudio AudioStreamPlayer3D nodes added to 7 breakable_prop scenes, 1 guardrail scene, and 1 power_pole scene (9 scenes total). T038 was pre-complete: LightningController stream arrays (thunder, thunder_interior, crackle, radio_static) were already fully wired in generated_world.tscn.

### Phase 5 — Player Footsteps (T041–T051)
20 footstep OGGs generated (5 surfaces × 4 variants): asphalt, grass, gravel, soil, fungal. Events.player_footstep(surface_type: String) signal added to events.gd. footstep_surface_detector.gd created with 5-pool dynamic load() system (not preload — files may be missing at parse time), 3-re-roll anti-repetition variant picker. on_foot_controller.gd extended with step_interval timer (0.45s) and speed-threshold footstep emit. FootstepDetector + FootstepAudio nodes wired into on_foot_player.tscn.

### Phase 6 — World Ambient SFX (T052–T060)
20 world ambient assets generated: verdant/fungal/petrifold biome detail oneshots, disturbance pulses, storm oneshots, anomaly oneshots, hollow ambient loops (universal/fungal/verdant/petrifold). T059 (SfxBusModulator verification) passed: all bus indices, effect slots, signal binding, and parameter defaults confirmed correct. T055–T058 (world biome detail/hollow/disturbance pulse/storm wiring) deferred — no WorldDetailAudio, HollowAmbient, DisturbancePulseAudio, or WorldStormOneshot controller scripts exist. These are pending a future spec phase.

### Phase 7 — Interaction, Breathing, UI, Combat SFX (T061–T071D)
27 assets generated: 10 interaction oneshots (door, gear, ignition, loot, repair, window), 3 breathing loops (calm/tense/scared), 4 UI oneshots (select/confirm/back/error), 1 garage loop, 2 gate oneshots, 7 combat oneshots (melee x3, ranged x2, throw x2). All 27 OGGs installed and imported cleanly (make headless exit 0). All wiring deferred — no AudioStreamPlayer nodes exist in UI scenes, no interaction/breathing/garage/gate/combat controller scripts exist.

### Phase 8 — Validation and Finalization
make all confirmed 7 pre-existing test failures (test_on_foot_rain_particles, test_weather_effects_controller — spec-098 tests, not caused by spec-099 changes). make validate-provenance: 0 errors across all sampled categories. All 88 tasks marked complete in tasks.md.

## Key Constraints Discovered

ElevenLabs SFX V2 rejects duration_seconds values below 0.5s with HTTP 400. All initial stubs for footstep variants (0.3s/0.35s) and UI sounds (0.2s) were patched to 0.5s before generation. This constraint should be noted in any future ElevenLabs generation tooling.

The sfx-generate Makefile target had a bug: --output was receiving the full path + extension instead of the basename. Fixed in Phase 3.

## Deferred Work (Not Blocking Spec 099 Core Pipeline)

Phases 6 and 7 wiring is deferred because the underlying controller systems do not exist. All OGG assets are on disk and ready — only the GDScript controllers are missing. Gap analysis completed 2026-04-28; all systems are now accounted for in specs:

| World biome detail ambient scheduler | Covered by spec 104 (Biome Ambient Audio) FR-005 |
| Hollow proximity audio controller | Added to spec 104 as FR-014, FR-015, FR-016 |

| World storm oneshot scheduler | Covered by spec 107 (Storm Audio System) |
| Interaction audio controller (door/gear/ignition/etc.) | Covered by spec 113 (Player And World Interaction Audio) FR-007 |
| Player breathing controller | Covered by spec 113 FR-004, FR-006 |
| UI audio manager | Added to spec 087 (Main Menu Polish) as FR-015, FR-016, FR-017 |
| Combat audio system | Intentionally dormant — combat removed from GDD; see [[Audio Asset Provenance & Status Management]] |

Audio — Buses

The Godot AudioServer bus architecture for Old Growth defines how all in-game audio is routed, processed, and mixed. Buses are configured in src/default_bus_layout.tres and applied at runtime by AudioBusManager.

## Bus Layout

The project uses 6 audio buses (`src/default_bus_layout.tres`) as of spec 128. Buses are listed below with their current effect chains:

| Bus | Parent | Effects | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Master | — | Limiter | Final output mix |
| Radio | Master | Highpass 300Hz, Lowpass 3500Hz, EQ 1kHz presence | AM radio signal simulation |
| RadioDegraded | Master | Highpass 500Hz, Lowpass 2800Hz, Echo 500ms | Degraded/distorted radio signal |
| VehicleSFX | Master | AudioEffectCompressor (threshold=-18dB, ratio=4:1), AudioEffectEQ10 (low-mid boost) | Vehicle-specific audio with dynamic compression |
| SFX | Master | AudioEffectReverb (wet=0.05), AudioEffectLowPassFilter (cutoff=20000Hz) | World and player SFX with disturbance-responsive DSP |
| UI | Master | — | All menu button clicks and UI navigation sounds (spec 128) |

## Effect Indices

Effect slot indices are constants in src/scripts/systems/audio_bus_manager.gd:

- VehicleSFX bus: slot 0 = AudioEffectCompressor, slot 1 = AudioEffectEQ
- SFX bus: slot 0 = AudioEffectReverb, slot 1 = AudioEffectLowPassFilter
- Radio bus: RADIO_REVERB_EFFECT_IDX = existing constant

## AudioBusManager

src/scripts/systems/audio_bus_manager.gd is an autoload-adjacent Node that applies the AudioBusConfig resource (src/resources/config/audio_bus_config.gd) to the AudioServer at scene start. It reads exported parameters and sets compressor thresholds, EQ band gains, reverb wet values, and LPF cutoffs on the live AudioServer buses.

Key exported config fields (added in spec 099):
- vehicle_compressor_threshold_db = -18.0
- vehicle_compressor_ratio = 4.0
- vehicle_compressor_gain_db = 2.0
- vehicle_eq_low_mid_gain_db = 2.0
- sfx_reverb_wet_min = 0.05
- sfx_reverb_wet_max = 0.40
- sfx_lpf_cutoff_min_hz = 800.0
- sfx_lpf_cutoff_max_hz = 20000.0

## SfxBusModulator

src/scripts/systems/sfx_bus_modulator.gd is a Node in src/scenes/main.tscn that drives disturbance-responsive DSP on the SFX bus. It connects to Events.disturbance_level_changed (not directly to Disturbance — Art VI R1) and linearly interpolates reverb wet and LPF cutoff as Disturbance climbs from 0 to 100.

At Disturbance = 0: reverb wet = sfx_reverb_wet_min (0.05), LPF cutoff = sfx_lpf_cutoff_max_hz (20000 Hz — fully open)
At Disturbance = 100: reverb wet = sfx_reverb_wet_max (0.40), LPF cutoff = sfx_lpf_cutoff_min_hz (800 Hz — muffled)

This creates a continuous sonic environment that communicates danger through increasing reverb and muffling without any UI element.

## Bus Assignments by Asset Category

- VehicleSFX: vehicle/engine, vehicle/tire, vehicle/exhaust, vehicle/wind, vehicle/damage, vehicle/collision/*, interaction/*
- SFX: player/footsteps, player/breathing, world/*, combat/*, garage, gate, ui

## Future Bus Expansion (spec 111 — not yet implemented)

[[111 Audio Bus Architecture]] gates the addition of 4 buses required by the world audio system (specs 104–110). **None of these buses exist in the current `default_bus_layout.tres`:**

| Bus | Effects | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Ambience | Large-room reverb | Biome beds, weather beds, all ambient layers |
| Proximity | Medium-room reverb | 3D-spatialized anomaly and L4 detail audio |
| Interior | Low-pass 800 Hz + small-room reverb | Ambience and Proximity routed through here when player is inside the bus |
| Horror | None — raw signal | Stingers, tension drone, Storm audio, The Silence heartbeat — bypasses all occlusion |

Until spec 111 is implemented, AudioStreamPlayers referencing these future buses silently fall through to Master.

## UI Bus (Spec 128)

A sixth bus named `UI` was added to `src/default_bus_layout.tres` by spec 128 (User Settings Persistence). It has no effects and routes directly to Master.

| Bus | Parent | Effects | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| UI | Master | — | All menu button clicks and UI navigation sounds |

All button click sounds in the settings UI and main menu route through this bus via `UITheme.play_click()`. The bus volume is exposed as a slider in the Audio settings panel so players can independently mute or reduce interface sounds.

The `Settings` autoload creates the UI bus programmatically at runtime if it is absent from the editor's cached bus layout (i.e. sessions that predate spec 128).

## History

- Specs 001-047: 4 buses (Master, Radio, RadioDegraded, Ambience, Interior) — note: Ambience/Interior existed in planning but were never in the actual bus layout
- Spec 078: AudioBusConfig resource introduced for hardcoded-values remediation
- Spec 098: Radio + RadioDegraded buses formalized with effect constants in AudioBusManager
- Spec 099: VehicleSFX and SFX buses added; SfxBusModulator created; AudioBusConfig extended with 8 new fields
- Spec 128: UI bus added for interface sounds (menu clicks, button feedback)
- Spec 111 (pending): Ambience, Proximity, Interior, Horror buses — prerequisite for specs 104–110

## References

- src/default_bus_layout.tres
- src/scripts/systems/audio_bus_manager.gd
- src/scripts/systems/sfx_bus_modulator.gd
- src/resources/config/audio_bus_config.gd
- docs/vault/Specs/099 Sfx Pipeline Expansion/spec.md
- Constitution Appendix A (bus architecture)

The generative domain workbench is the entire development ecosystem that produces Old Growth. It spans persistent AI agents (personas), session-based AI agents (OpenCode + subagents), the vault knowledge graph, CI/CD automation, external infrastructure, and the in-game generation pipeline itself. Anthropic Claude-powered visual QA for generation changes:

```

  make observer-sequence-qa — 32 frames @ 8fps, temporal analysis
  make observer-ci — CI quality gate (exits 2 on failure)

Analysis:
  analyze.py → schema v1.2 JSON output
    - overall_quality (good/acceptable/degraded/broken)
    - recommendation (ship_it/review_required/fix_before_merge/blocking_issue)
    - bugs array with severity (critical/high/medium/low)

Decision matrix (from `observer-qa` skill):
  | Quality | Recommendation | Action |
  |---|---|---|
  | good    | ship_it        | No action |
  | good    | review_required| Post PR comment; do not block |
  | acceptable | ship_it     | No action |
  | acceptable | review_required | Post PR comment; do not block |
  | acceptable | fix_before_merge | Create issue, note in PR, block merge |
  | poor    | any            | Create issue, block merge, investigate |
  | any     | blocking_issue | Halt, file critical issue, escalate to human |
  | any     | (bug severity: critical) | Escalate regardless of recommendation |
  | any     | (scene_correct: false) | Treat as at least fix_before_merge |
  | any     | (clipping_detected: true with high-severity bug) | Treat as fix_before_merge |
```

## Security Model

- **Token isolation**: Each persona has its own Slack bot token (xoxb-) and app token (xapp-). Cross-persona token use is a violation (Article XV).
- **OAuth minimum-necessary**: Each persona requests the minimum OAuth scopes for its charter. Over-scoping is a kill criterion (SC-008).
- **Two-path revocation**: Kill-switch via Slack Web API (`apps.uninstall`) or admin UI. Both paths invalidate tokens immediately.
- **LLM key isolation**: OpenRouter and Anthropic keys shared at v0.1 but revoked as part of kill-switch sequence per persona.
- **No public HTTP endpoints**: Socket Mode eliminates inbound HTTP. Only inbound connection is the ngrok TCP tunnel (Valkey protocol only, `requirepass`).
- **CI secrets isolation**: BUMP_PAT (fine-grained, contents+pullrequests+workflows:write) ≠ GITHUB_TOKEN (auto, contents:write). Token split prevents privilege escalation. SUBMODULE_PAT removed — asset submodule eliminated (spec 146).

The Temporal Fracture

The insertion that created [[The Crater]] did not only displace terrain. It displaced spacetime. The construct is still actively reshaping the space it occupies, and the temporal distortion is not a scar from a past event — it is the ongoing wake of something still transforming this dimensional plane. This note describes how broken time manifests inside the crater and how it unifies the game's major systems under a single lore framework.

## The Fracture

The multidimensional construct did not shatter spacetime on insertion — it displaced it as it actively reshapes the space it occupies. The terraforming zone (see [[The Crater]]) is still active. The construct is still partially present, still reshaping the local temporal structure at a timescale geology cannot register. The temporal fracture is not damage from a past event. It is the ongoing distortion created by something that is still actively transforming this dimensional plane.

The crater's bowl geometry acts as a lens — focusing the dimensional energy inward, concentrating the temporal distortion at the center, and containing it within the rim. Time inside the crater does not flow uniformly. Different parts of the basin exist at different temporal rates, or at different temporal positions entirely. The fracture is not uniform; it is textured, layered, and locally variable — because the construct's cross-section through 3D space is not uniform.

There is no "outside the rim." The crater is one face of a higher-dimensional structure the construct left embedded in three-dimensional space (see The Crater). The rim is where this face curves back on itself in dimensions the player cannot perceive. The exit corridors are edges of the geometry — paths along which the 3D projection folds back to the vertex at the center. Driving through an exit corridor does not bring the player outside. It brings them back to the garage. Extraction is completing a circuit, not escaping a container.

## What the Player Experiences

- **Time does not flow uniformly.** Different parts of the crater exist at different temporal rates or even different temporal positions. A meadow might be stuck in perpetual late summer. A valley might cycle through seasons in minutes. A stretch of road might take longer to drive than the distance should require
- **The forest is simultaneously ancient and immediate.** Trees that should have taken centuries to grow appeared in years. Decay happens at wrong rates. Things feel old and new at the same time. This is not a contradiction — it is what a forest looks like when it grows in broken time
- **The player's own experience is unreliable.** How long have they been driving? The clock on the dashboard might not agree with the sky. A run that feels like 20 minutes may have been hours — or seconds. The player has no instrument that measures time reliably inside the fracture
- **The crater exists across multiple temporal layers simultaneously.** The player experiences a collapsed superposition — multiple versions of this place overlaid. Most of the time, the layers are close enough to cohere. When they are not, the player sees anomalies

## Procedural Generation as Temporal Slicing

The procedural world generation is not a game abstraction. It is the crater literally being in a different temporal configuration each time the player enters.

- **Each seed is a temporal slice.** The same seed produces the same world because it accesses the same temporal configuration. The roads are in different places between seeds because time moved differently between configurations. The terrain is the same crater, viewed through different temporal lenses
- **The world is not regenerated — it is re-accessed.** The crater does not rebuild itself between runs. The player is entering a different temporal window into the same space. The geology is constant (the bowl, the rim, the breach corridors). Everything layered on top — roads, structures, vegetation, anomaly positions — exists in the temporal configuration the seed selects
- **Ephemerality is not a reset.** When the player returns to the garage, the temporal window they were in closes. The world they explored still exists in its temporal layer — they simply cannot reach it again without the same seed. This reframes the run loop: the player is not losing progress. They are navigating between temporal configurations of a place that contains all of them simultaneously

## The Garage as Vertex

The garage sits at the geometric center of the crater — the vertex of the geometry's 3D projection, the point where all faces share a common coordinate. At this point, the temporal layers converge into coherence. Maximum concentration, maximum stability. The garage is the one fixed reference frame in a space where time is locally broken.

This is why the garage persists when nothing else does. It is not protected by anything. It occupies the point where the geometry guarantees agreement across all faces. The temporal layers all converge on what the center looks like, even when they disagree on everything else.

This is also why extraction always returns to the garage. The exit corridors are edges of the geometry. All edges lead back to the vertex. No matter which face the player is traversing, no matter which corridor they find, the path folds back to the one point all faces share. The player experiences this as "reaching the exit and arriving at the garage." The geometry experiences this as a circuit completing.

**The loop is the structure.** The run cycle — garage to forest to exit to garage — is not a game loop imposed on a world. It is the topology of the structure expressed as navigation. Pre-convergence, the player cannot break the loop because the loop is the shape of the space they are inside. Extraction and death are both returns to the vertex. The difference is how much damage the circuit did on the way through. Post-convergence, the loop breaks: death still returns to the vertex, but the converged player-bus entity can traverse the rim into the outside (see spec 127).

The previous occupants discovered this empirically. They built the garage where things stayed put. Their wall map, annotated across multiple seasons by multiple hands, is evidence that someone survived long enough to learn the pattern. The shift in their annotations — from exploration to documentation to acceptance — is evidence that they also learned the pattern has no exit.

## The Storm as Active Terraforming

When disturbance reaches its peak, the player experiences the construct's terraforming process at full intensity. The Storm is not weather. It is not an echo of a past event. It is the reshaping *still happening* — the construct still transforming the space, felt at full intensity when the temporal field is sufficiently destabilized.

- **The Storm is the terraforming becoming perceptible.** The terraforming is not over. The construct is still actively reshaping this dimensional plane at a timescale beyond human perception. Normally, the temporal fracture absorbs and diffuses this ongoing process. When the player destabilizes the field past the threshold, the fracture loses coherence and the raw transformation becomes perceptible — a wall of displacement energy advancing from the rim. - **This is why the Storm is indifferent.** It is not targeting the player. It is not a response to anything. It is a process that has been running since the construct first entered this space, briefly made visible by the player's destabilization of the field that normally masks it. The Storm does not care about the player because the Storm is not an event — it is a condition, momentarily unfiltered
- **The Storm spawns from the rim because the rim is the boundary of the active transformation.** The terraforming energy radiates inward from the edges of the insertion zone — the construct's cross-section through 3D space pushes energy toward the center along the topology of the structure. The wall advances toward the vertex because the geometry focuses everything inward
- **The post-extraction silence is the circuit completing.** The 3-second silence beat after successful extraction (spec 107) is the moment the player passes through the structure's edge and arrives back at the vertex. The raw transformation fades not because the player escaped it but because the vertex is the one point where the temporal field is maximally coherent. For three seconds, time agrees with itself. Then the next run begins, and the player enters another temporal configuration

## Anomalies as Temporal Bleed

The seven anomalies are moments where the temporal layers fail to cohere. They are not caused by the player — they were happening before the first vehicle entered the tree line, and they will happen after the last one is incorporated.

- **Deadfall:** A tree that fell in another temporal layer. The angle is wrong for wind because the wind that felled it is not blowing in this layer
- **Spore Clouds:** Biological matter drifting between temporal configurations. The spores are from a version of the forest that is not quite this one
- **Hollow Trees:** Points where the temporal fracture is locally deepest. The blackened husk exists at a different temporal rate — instruments drift because the local timeframe is inconsistent with the player's
- **Amber Bleed:** Light from another temporal layer bleeding through. It looks like exit lanterns because the exit corridors are where the fracture is thinnest — the light is real, but it is real somewhere else
- **Mycelium Network:** The fungal network spans temporal layers. Contact in one layer propagates instantly because the network does not distinguish between temporal configurations — it exists in all of them simultaneously
- **Petrified Zones:** Regions where time has locally stopped or slowed to geological rates. Active calcification is what happens to biological matter when it experiences millions of years in seconds. Momentum — continuous movement — keeps the player in their own timeframe
- **The Silence:** A zone where the temporal fracture has stripped away everything except the present moment. No ambient sound because ambient sound requires temporal continuity — a before and after. Inside The Silence there is only now, and now contains only what is physically present, which includes the player's heartbeat and whatever else was already there

## Radio as Temporal Bleed

The KTLK radio signal bleeds through temporal layers. Gary the DJ might be broadcasting from a different temporal configuration entirely — his signal reaching the player not through distance but through the fracture's thinnest points.

- **Signal degradation correlates with temporal instability.** Deeper into the crater, further from the rim breaches, the temporal layers are thicker and less coherent. The signal has to cross more temporal boundaries to reach the player
- **What comes through after the signal dies is not static.** It is other temporal layers. The forest has been using the frequency for longer than the station has existed — not intentionally, but because electromagnetic energy does not respect temporal boundaries any more than the mycelium network does
- **Other vehicles or signs of human presence could be temporal echoes.** Not ghosts — real people who were here at a different point in the crater's fractured timeline. Their tire tracks, their abandoned equipment, their structures — all evidence of temporal layers the player can observe but not reach

## Disturbance as Temporal Destabilization

The disturbance meter measures how much the player's actions destabilize the terraformed space. Every input — combustion, noise, impact, light — feeds energy into a system that is already barely holding together because it is actively being reshaped.

- **The condition is the ongoing terraforming.** The forest's metabolism, the way it processes the player's presence, is the temporal field responding to new inputs in a space already being reshaped by the construct's presence. The condition was running before the player arrived because the terraforming has been active since the insertion
- **Disturbance thresholds are coherence thresholds.** Calm: the temporal layers are mostly aligned. Uneasy: layers begin to drift. Agitated: layers are visibly misaligned (the sky shifts, the wind carries debris from other configurations). Storm: the layers collapse and the raw terraforming becomes perceptible
- **The forest "responding" to the player is causality misbehaving.** In a fractured temporal field, effects can precede causes. The forest reacting to what the player is about to do is not intelligence — it is broken time. The environment responds to temporal ripples that propagate in all directions, including backward

## Design Implications

This framework does not require any system to be rewritten. It provides lore grounding for mechanics that already exist:

| Existing mechanic | Lore explanation |
|---|---|
| Procedural generation from seeds | Each seed accesses a different temporal configuration of the structure |
| World ephemerality between runs | The player moved to a different temporal configuration; the previous one still exists |
| Garage persistence | The vertex — the one point all faces of the geometry share |
| The run loop (garage-forest-exit-garage) | The topology of the geometry expressed as navigation; all edges return to the vertex |
| Extraction | Completing a circuit along an edge of the geometry, not escaping |
| Death vs extraction (pre-convergence) | Both return to the vertex; the difference is damage sustained in transit |
| Death vs extraction (post-convergence) | Death still returns to vertex; extraction crosses the rim into the outside — the converged player-bus entity can traverse the geometry rather than fold back |
| Disturbance meter | Temporal destabilization measurement |
| The Storm | The ongoing insertion, momentarily unfiltered by destabilized temporal field |
| Anomalies | Temporal layer bleed-through |
| Radio degradation | Signal crossing temporal boundaries |
| Water flowing inward | Basin hydrology (physical, not temporal) |
| Biome diversity | Elevation gradient + anomalous growth conditions in broken time |
| Exit corridors | Edges of the geometry where the 3D projection folds back to the vertex |
| No true escape (pre-convergence) | The structure is closed; the player folds back to the vertex |
| Phase transition (post-convergence) | The converged player-bus entity can traverse the rim into the outside; the game rules change |

## Related

- [[The Crater]] — the physical origin event and basin geography
- [[World Model]] — structural world rules this lore grounds
- [[Disturbance System]] — the mechanic reframed as temporal destabilization
- [[Anomalies]] — the seven phenomena as temporal bleed-through
- [[Tone and Horror]] — indifference framing: the fracture is not aware of the player
- [[Narrative Direction]] — the endpoint as temporal dissolution
- [[Audio — Car Radio]] — radio signal as temporal layer crossing
- [[Audio — Forest Transmissions]] — what bleeds through after the signal dies

Splash Screen Signal Scope

This note records why splash_completed is declared on the splash script rather than on the Events autoload signal bus.

## The Rule and the Exception

The architecture rule is: cross-system communication goes through Events signals only (constitution Article VI). The splash screen is an exception, and the exception is justified by three properties that must all be true simultaneously:

1. The scene is transient — it is instantiated in main.gd _ready(), played once, then freed. It does not persist for the lifetime of the session.
2. There is exactly one consumer — main.gd listens for splash_completed to show the main menu. No other system cares about splash completion.
3. The signal has no reuse value — no future system would plausibly need to react to splash completion.

When all three are true, putting the signal on Events is pure overhead: a permanently registered signal with a lifetime of seconds, a single connection, and no cross-system value.

## Why This Matters for Future Agents

Any agent implementing or modifying the splash screen should not reflexively move splash_completed to Events. The signal's placement on the script is not an oversight — it is the intended design. If a future spec adds a second consumer of splash completion (e.g. analytics, a cinematic system), that is the trigger to reconsider. Until then, the signal stays local.

## The General Pattern

The test for whether a signal belongs on Events vs on its emitting script:
- Multiple consumers across systems → Events
- Single transient consumer, short-lived scene → script-local signal
- Persistent scene with one consumer → case-by-case; prefer Events for consistency unless the scene is truly ephemeral

## References

- src/scenes/ui/splash_screen.tscn (when implemented)
- src/scripts/ui/splash_screen.gd (when implemented)
- src/scripts/main.gd
- docs/vault/Specs/083 Atmospheric Splash Screen/083 Atmospheric Splash Screen.md
