Linux Release Architecture — CI Topology and Platform Independence

The release workflow must handle macOS and Linux as parallel, independent paths — one platform's export failure must not block the other. This required changes to the `sign-and-release` job topology and introduced a cross-platform AppImage pipeline.

## Decision

### Multi-platform Sign-and-Release Topology

The `sign-and-release` job uses `if: always() && needs.check-version.outputs.version_changed == 'true'` with `needs: [check-version, export-universal, export-linux]`. macOS-specific steps (code signing, notarization, DMG creation) are guarded by `if: needs.export-universal.result == 'success'`. Linux artifacts are downloaded and processed conditionally with `if: needs.export-linux.result == 'success'`.

### Independent R2 Upload per Platform

Each export job uploads its own artifacts to R2 independently. The Linux job (`export-linux`) calls `upload-to-r2.sh --platform linux` without gating on `sign-and-release`. This ensures the Linux AppImage reaches `downloads.playoldgrowth.com` even if the macOS signing pipeline fails.

### AppImage for Release, .zip for CI

Godot's Linux export produces a .zip (binary + .pck). For release artifacts, `appimagetool` wraps this into a self-contained AppImage using `AppImage/AppImageKit-action@v1`. The CI smoke test (`linux-export-smoke`) uses the raw .zip export — no AppImage wrapping needed since the test only validates the export pipeline, not the final distribution format.

## Rationale

A shared GitHub Release with conditional artifact attachment provides a single download page per version. Decoupling R2 upload from `sign-and-release` ensures the Linux download is always available even if macOS signing infrastructure fails (Apple Developer ID certificate expiry, notarization outage).

## Alternatives Considered

- Separate signing-and-release job per platform (duplicates GitHub Release creation logic)
- One release per platform (splits version history across multiple release objects)
- macOS job owns all publishing (creates single point of failure for both platforms)

## Consequences

- `sign-and-release` runs on `macos-latest` regardless of outcome — consumes runner time even when only Linux succeeds
- The workflow artifact `app-linux` must be compatible with macOS (AppImage files are cross-platform)
- Release notes are dynamically generated based on which platforms produced artifacts

Host-Tools MCP Server Launchd Lifecycle

The host-tools MCP server on port 9105 is owned by launchd via `com.oldgrowth.host-mcp.plist`. The `mcp-setup` command must never attempt to check port availability or start its own server instance — it should verify server health and proceed with tool attachment.

## Background

The `cmd_mcp_setup()` function in `scripts/personas/system-manager.py` originally used `socket.bind()` to check if port 9105 was free. On a clean boot, launchd starts the host-tools MCP server via `com.oldgrowth.host-mcp.plist` (RunAtLoad + KeepAlive), so the port is always in use — causing `socket.bind()` to fail and `make recovery` to exit with "Port 9105 is already in use."

This was a design mismatch: launchd owns the server lifecycle (start, keep alive, restart on crash), and `mcp-setup` only needs to verify the server is healthy and attach MCP tools to Letta agents. The port-conflict check was an artifact from an earlier design where `mcp-setup` was expected to start its own server.

## Fix

The port-conflict check was replaced with a two-phase health check:

1. Hit `GET /health` on port 9105. If the server responds, skip to tool attachment.
2. If unreachable, attempt `launchctl bootstrap` (or `load`) against the launchd plist, wait up to ~6 seconds for the server to come up, then proceed.

This handles every scenario: normal boot (launchd has it running), plist unloaded (auto-start via launchctl), server crashed (auto-restart via launchd).

## Related

- `scripts/personas/system-manager.py` — `cmd_mcp_setup()` and `_ensure_host_mcp_server()`
- `personas/host_mcp_server.py` — the server itself, listens on 9105
- `personas/launchd/com.oldgrowth.host-mcp.plist` — launchd plist managing the server
- `personas/config.py` — `HOST_TOOLS_CALLBACK_PORT = 9105` constant

## References

- `scripts/personas/system-manager.py` — `_ensure_host_mcp_server()` function (lines ~302-380)
- `personas/host_mcp_server.py` — `/health` endpoint implementation (lines 1049-1069)
- `personas/launchd/com.oldgrowth.host-mcp.plist` — launchd plist with RunAtLoad + KeepAlive

Vehicle — Samba Exterior

> **⚠️ PRE-068 NOTE — asset paths and material resource names will be verified when spec 068 ships.**
> Material `.tres` file paths are proposed targets. After 068 ships the purchased model, confirm resource names against the actual committed geometry. Spec 082 will reconcile.

This note covers PBR material specs for all exterior surfaces. For the palette derivation rationale and archival paint code research, see [[Vehicle Palette Materials and Dimensions Discovery]]. For dimensional anchors (panel locations, window sizes), see [[Art/Vehicle — Samba Dimensions]].

## Exterior panel diagram

![[_meta/attachments/vehicle/panels_exterior_callout.svg]]

## Hero palette (exterior)

| Slot | Name | sRGB hex | Linear RGB | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `hero_cream_upper` | `#D9D3BE` | `(0.675, 0.615, 0.513)` | Primary upper body paint |
| 2 | `hero_teal_lower` | `#3F6E66` | `(0.047, 0.154, 0.138)` | Primary lower body paint |
| 3 | `weathered_cream_upper` | `#C9C2AB` | `(0.581, 0.529, 0.418)` | Sun-faded upper (roof peaks, raised surfaces) |
| 4 | `weathered_teal_lower` | `#355A56` | `(0.032, 0.103, 0.097)` | Sun-faded lower (hood front, running boards, rockers) |
| 5 | `trim_beltline` | `#B5B0A3` | `(0.453, 0.421, 0.363)` | Chrome decorative strip with tarnish |
| 6 | `vw_roundel_chrome` | `#D4D0C5` | `(0.646, 0.613, 0.546)` | VW badge and bright chrome trim |
| 7 | `shadow_deep` | `#1B2E2A` | `(0.009, 0.028, 0.024)` | AO reference / deep crevice shadow colour |

**Archival anchor**: Option B — L289 Blue White / L380 Turquoise. Hero palette is intentionally adjusted from archival codes for moodboard alignment; values above are the production target, not the factory codes. See [[Vehicle Palette Materials and Dimensions Discovery]] for the full archival baseline.

**Two-tone boundary rule**: The paint boundary is a hard seam at the chrome beltline strip. Paint does NOT gradient-blend. Model the beltline as a separate bevelled feature; assign upper and lower paint as two distinct material slots.

## Painted body

Covers: nose cone, hood front, all fenders, all side panels, roof panels, engine hatch, all doors, running boards where painted.

**Panel IDs**: `nose_cone`, `hood_front`, `engine_hatch`, `panel_front_lower`, `fender_front_left`, `fender_front_right`, `fender_rear_left`, `fender_rear_right`, `panel_side_left_front/mid/rear`, `panel_side_right_front/mid/rear`, `door_left_front`, `door_right_front`, `door_rear_left`, `door_rear_right`, `panel_rear_upper`, `roof_panel_front/mid/rear`, `running_board_left`, `running_board_right`.

### PBR rules (all states)
- **Metalness**: 0.0 — non-metallic nitrocellulose lacquer. No metallic flake.
- **Clearcoat**: DISABLED — 1963 paint was not clearcoated.
- **Two-tone**: hard seam at chrome beltline; two separate material instances above and below.

### Clean state
| Property | Upper | Lower |
|---|---|---|
| Albedo | `hero_cream_upper` | `hero_teal_lower` |
| Roughness | 0.55–0.65 | 0.55–0.65 |
| Normal | Subtle panel-seam + minor hand-beaten imperfections (period-correct) | Same |
| AO | Panel-seam and wheel-arch bake | Same |

### Worn state (default Old Growth game state)
| Property | Upper | Lower |
|---|---|---|
| Albedo | `hero_cream_upper` → `weathered_cream_upper` blend (60/40 worn) | `hero_teal_lower` → `weathered_teal_lower` blend |
| Roughness | 0.65–0.80 (lost gloss; worse on horizontal surfaces) | Same |
| Normal | Paint chips at panel edges, fender tops, hood corners; minor hail-type dimples on horizontal surfaces | Same |
| Weathering mask | World-up normal + panel edge proximity + wheel-well proximity | Same |

### Damaged state (heavy wear)
| Property | Upper | Lower |
|---|---|---|
| Albedo | `weathered_cream_upper` + primer `#8A7E68` in exposed spots + rust `#7A4A2C` at edges | `weathered_teal_lower` + exposed metal |
| Roughness | 0.80–0.95 (matte, oxidised) | Same |
| Metalness | 0.0 on paint; 0.7 on bare metal | Same |
| Normal | Deep paint loss patches, real dents, bent panels, visible panel seam displacement | Same |
| Rust layer | Colour `#7A4A2C`, roughness 0.95, metalness 0.2 (oxidised iron has partial metallic character) | Same |

**Wet state modifier**: roughness drops ~0.10; specular rises. See `src/assets/shaders/rain_on_glass.gdshader` for wet-surface shader reference.

## Chrome trim

Decorative chrome bright trim: beltline strip, window surrounds, VW roundel badge, door handles, headlight bezels, bumper overriders, side mirror housings, radio fascia bezel.

| State | Albedo | Roughness | Metalness | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Clean | `vw_roundel_chrome` (#D4D0C5), slightly cooler | 0.05–0.15 | 1.0 | Mirror polish |
| Worn (default) | Same + subtle yellowed patches | 0.20–0.40 | 0.85 | Light oxidation |
| Damaged | `#A09A88` (dull yellowed); rust blooms `#7A4A2C` at pitting | 0.60–0.85 | 0.55 | Pitted chrome |

Period chrome is triple-plated (copper-nickel-chrome). When pitted, copper undertones appear — add warm pink hint at pitting damage sites.

## Bumpers

Front and rear bumpers: painted steel tube body with chrome overrider bars. The bumper tube is upper-body-colour; overriders are chrome-plated.

| Part | Clean | Worn | Damaged |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tube albedo | `hero_cream_upper` | Scratches exposing primer `#3A342C` | Heavy scratches, exposed metal, rust |
| Tube roughness | 0.55 | 0.70 | 0.85 |
| Tube metalness | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 (+ 0.7 on exposed metal) |
| Overriders albedo | `vw_roundel_chrome` | Dull | Pitted chrome + oxide |
| Overriders roughness | 0.08 | 0.25 | 0.70 |
| Overriders metalness | 1.0 | 0.9 | 0.5 |

Bumper mount brackets behind the tube are unpainted black-phosphate steel and can show through damaged areas.

## Rubber seals

Window gaskets, door weatherstripping, windshield perimeter seal.

| State | Albedo | Roughness | Metalness | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Clean | `#1A1A1A` deep matte black | 0.90–0.95 | 0.0 | Essentially Lambertian rubber |
| Worn | `#252525` grey-brown from UV | 0.85 | 0.0 | Slight hardening, surface craze |
| Damaged | Cracked rubber, white chalking visible | 0.80 | 0.0 | Perished rubber look |

> [!note] Moss accumulation priority: rubber seals are high-priority contamination zones in the Verdant biome — seams and gaskets trap moisture and organic material. See [[Art/Vehicle — Contamination]].

## Glass (19 panels)

Windshield (upper + lower split panes), 6 side windows, 8 skylights, 2 rear corner windows, 1 rear window. All flat or mildly curved automotive glass.

| State | Albedo alpha | Roughness | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Clean | 0.08 (nearly transparent, subtle green tint from period iron-content glass) | 0.0 | Mirror-smooth |
| Worn (default) | 0.12 (internal haze + water spot overlay) | 0.05 | Water spots, dirt streaks |
| Damaged (cracked) | Crack-pattern overlay as albedo (white lines on alpha) | 0.15 at cracks | |
| Damaged (shattered) | Crack pattern + additional displacement | 0.15 | |

> [!warning] **Do NOT replace the existing rain/wiper shader stack.**
> `src/scripts/bus/windshield_rain.gd` and `src/resources/windshield_rain_material.tres` are live in the codebase. Phase 3 glass materials must integrate with these, not replace them. The rain shader handles dynamic water droplets and wiper interaction. See [[Systems/Vehicle — Samba]] for the art integration constraint.

Period laminated windshield glass has a slight green tint from iron content in the glass — this is period correct. Apply a subtle green-cast transparency.

## Tyres

Four 5.60-15 bias-ply tyres on 15 in steel rims with painted hubcaps.

| State | Albedo | Roughness | Metalness | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Clean | `#1A1A1A` deep matte black | 0.88 | 0.0 | Narrow bias-ply tread (NOT modern aggressive tread) |
| Worn (default) | `#202020` greyed from road dust | 0.85 | 0.0 | |
| Damaged (flat/detached) | Shredded rubber texture; exposed steel belt | 0.80 | 0.3 (steel belt) | At `damaged_threshold = 0.3` the tyre visually deflates |

Period tyre sidewalls show "5.60-15" or "165R15" branding plus manufacturer name. **Avoid modern all-terrain or aggressive tread.** This is a narrow-rib bias-ply profile.

## Texture variety sets (Phase 3)

Five full PBR variety sets (BaseColor, Roughness, Metallic, NormalMap) needed for the exterior panel groups:

| Variety | Description |
|---|---|
| `weathered` | Sun fading, chalky paint, minor surface rust at panel edges |
| `forest_worn` | Moss at seals, lichen on lower panels, sap streaks, bark scrapes |
| `muddy` | Mud splatter on lower panels and wheel arches |
| `rain_wet` | Wet sheen, water droplets, rain streaks, dark wet wheel arches |
| `deep_forest` | Heavy moss, fungal patches, years of accumulation |

## Godot material targets (proposed)

| Resource | Albedo slot | Roughness | Metalness |
|---|---|---|---|
| `van_body_upper.tres` | `hero_cream_upper` | 0.65 | 0.0 |
| `van_body_lower.tres` | `hero_teal_lower` | 0.65 | 0.0 |
| `van_chrome_trim.tres` | `vw_roundel_chrome` | 0.10 | 1.0 |
| `van_bumper_tube.tres` | `hero_cream_upper` | 0.55 | 0.0 |
| `van_glass.tres` | Color(1,1,1,0.08) | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| `van_tyre.tres` | `#1A1A1A` | 0.88 | 0.0 |
| `van_rubber_seal.tres` | `#1A1A1A` | 0.92 | 0.0 |

Spec 098 Weather Effects Implementation — Apr 25 2026

Implementation session for spec 098 (Weather Effects Completion). All 12 phases executed via parallel agent delegation in a single session.

## What Was Built

### Windshield SOLID Hierarchy
- `windshield_overlay_base.gd` — abstract base (push_error guards on 5 abstract methods)
- `rain_overlay.gd` — migrated all logic from deleted `windshield_rain.gd`
- `snow_overlay.gd` — opaque white accumulation (LIGHT_SNOW→0.3, HEAVY_SNOW→0.7, BLIZZARD→1.0)
- `spore_film_overlay.gd` + `spore_film.gdshader` — amber-blue film, smear-not-clear wiper behavior
- `frost_overlay.gd` + `windshield_frost.gdshader` — 60s delay, edge-inward growth, wiper-immune
- `windshield_controller.gd` — coordinator routing all 4 overlays

### Particle Systems
- `weather_effects_controller.gd` — Node3D with QualityTier enum; snow/spore/ash GPUParticles3D
- `on_foot_weather_particles.gd` — mirrors on_foot_rain_particles.gd for snow/spore/ash/hail

### Audio Controllers
- `wind_audio_controller.gd` — interior/exterior split, volume = lerpf(WIND_SILENT_DB, WIND_MAX_DB, wind)
- `dead_calm_audio_controller.gd` — sub-bass fade-in/-out at -45 dB on Ambience bus
- `instrument_disruption_handler.gd` — FLICKER/OSCILLATE patterns, graceful no-op when needles absent

### Game Systems
- `lightning_controller.gd` — seeded RNG (seed + 9173), discharge timer, WorldEnvironment flash, thunder audio, instrument_disruption_changed emission, ELECTRICAL_STORM crackle + radio static
- `on_foot_controller.gd` — wind_speed_penalty_scale + _wind_mult, get_target_speed() × _wind_mult
- `rain_audio_controller.gd` — additive hail audio branch (is_hail + THUNDERSTORM)
- `rain_particles_controller.gd` — hail particle swap during THUNDERSTORM+is_hail
- `fog_system.gd` — ELECTRICAL_STORM_SKY_COLOR tween (Color(0.25, 0.0, 0.4)) over 3.0s
- `wet_road_controller.gd` — ash road coating via albedo lerp + roughness delta
- `disturbance_storm_audio.gd` — preloaded _STORM_ROAR_STREAM const

### Assets
- 16 audio placeholder .ogg files in `src/assets/audio/ambient/weather/`
- `src/assets/audio/ambient/weather/gold/.gdignore` — non-shippable gold masters excluded
- `src/resources/windshield_snow_material.tres` — snow shader material

- `WeatherEffectsController` (Node3D + script) with `SnowParticles`, `SporeParticles`, `AshParticles` (GPUParticles3D, particle materials assigned, NodePaths wired)

Vehicle — Dashboard

The Samba's dashboard is Old Growth's HUD. Fuel gauge, speedometer, tachometer, gear indicator, battery gauge, and the radio — all amber-glow instruments mounted on the physical dashboard geometry. There is no non-diegetic UI overlay during driving. The dashboard *is* the UI. Per Article XII-G.

## Overview

The dashboard implements the complete driving-mode information layer: vehicle state (speed, RPM, gear, fuel, battery), vehicle systems (headlights, wipers, dome light), and the radio (see [[Audio — Car Radio]]). Amber glow, analog needles, and tactile diegetic interaction — this is the entire HUD.

## Design Intent

Per Article XII-G and [[Diegesis Thread]]: **diegetic UI is the commitment**. Any non-diegetic UI element breaks the frame the Samba provides. The dashboard exists to carry every piece of information the player needs without breaking diegesis.

The amber glow is an identity mark (World Bible Section 3). It signals *inside the bus* to the player — warm, familiar, close. In contrast to the forest's colors (see [[Palettes]]), amber is the Samba's color. The Amber Bleed anomaly (see [[Anomalies]]) deliberately borrows this visual language for diegetic confusion.

## Key Decisions

### Instruments — analog, not digital

- **Fuel gauge** — needle, amber backlight
- **Speedometer** — needle, analog dial
- **Tachometer** — needle, redline marked
- **Gear indicator** — discrete indicator (forward / reverse)
- **Battery gauge** — needle; goes yellow under electrical stress

### Dashboard lights

- **Headlights indicator** — on when headlights active
- **High beam indicator** — distinct from normal headlight
- **Wiper state indicator** — off / slow / fast
- **Dome light** — interior, toggleable when focused (`E` per [[Controls]])

### Radio as part of the dashboard

The radio is physically on the dashboard. Look at it to activate tuning controls. All radio state (power, station, volume) is shown via its physical knobs and dial — no overlay, no menu.

### No overlay during driving

No healthbar overlay. No minimap. No quest marker. No disturbance meter (Article X intentionally hides it). No ammo counter. Driving is pure diegesis.

### Exception: loading and menu

The main menu and the loading screen ARE non-diegetic (Article XII-G explicitly permits this — diegesis applies to in-world gameplay, not to the frame around it). Once the run begins, diegesis takes over.

### Electrical system is fragile

The World Bible notes: "The electrical system is old and prone to failure when exposed to extreme stress." Under stress (water intrusion via destroyed panels, anomaly proximity like Hollow Trees), dashboard instruments can drift, flicker, or temporarily fail. The needles go first — they "drift to meaningless positions, not zeroing out but genuinely confused, pointing at things that aren't there."

### Dashboard-radio interaction flow

Looking at the radio (raycast from camera hits the radio mesh) activates the radio input context. Controls (`E` toggle power, `T`/`Y` tune, `=`/`-` volume) affect the radio while the look is held. Looking away deactivates the context; general driving inputs resume.

## Implementation

Primary code references (all under `src/scripts/bus/`):
- `src/scripts/bus/bus_radio.gd` — radio (see [[Audio — Car Radio]])
- `src/scripts/bus/radio_knob_power.gd`, `src/scripts/bus/radio_knob_tuning.gd` — diegetic radio controls
- `src/scripts/bus/mirror_system.gd` — rearview mirrors
- `src/scripts/bus/steering_wheel.gd` — steering wheel animation
- `src/scripts/bus/headlight_system.gd` — headlights + high beams
- `src/scripts/bus/wiper_system.gd` — wipers + state machine
- `src/scripts/bus/dome_light_control.gd` — interior dome light
- `src/scripts/bus/engine_audio.gd` — engine audio tied to RPM/gear
- `src/scripts/bus/windshield_rain.gd`, `rain_particles_controller.gd`, `rain_audio_controller.gd`, `splash_particles.gd` — windshield rain + splash
- `src/scripts/bus/interior_camera.gd`, `chase_camera.gd` — cameras
- `src/scenes/bus/samba_bus.tscn` — dashboard geometry lives in the Samba scene
- `src/scripts/ui/` — UI elements that sit on top of the dashboard (menu, loading)

Signals consumed:
- `Events.headlight_state_changed`
- `Events.wiper_state_changed`
- `Events.radio_power_changed`, `Events.radio_station_changed`
- Various vehicle-state signals from GEVP

## Test Coverage

- `src/tests/unit/test_bus_panel.gd` — panel data integrity
- `src/tests/unit/test_headlight_system.gd`, `test_wiper_system.gd`, `test_windshield_rain.gd` — peripherals
- `src/tests/unit/test_mirror_system.gd` — mirrors
- `src/tests/unit/test_steering_wheel.gd` — steering wheel
- `src/tests/unit/test_engine_audio.gd` — engine audio

Core Mechanics

The mechanical and systems spine of Old Growth: the run loop, player stats, vehicle specifications, resources, garage systems, on-foot handling, UI philosophy, save system, and progression framework. Where [[World Model]] establishes structure and [[Tone and Horror]] establishes register, this note captures the authoritative mechanical values. All values marked `[PENDING]` require playtesting to finalize.

## Overview

Every mechanic serves three design pillars. When a proposed system conflicts, the system changes, not the pillars.

- **Flesh as Horror.** Player body and bus body are both subject to irreversible change. Damage cumulates and is visible. The condition crosses run boundaries in both — the bus through contamination, the player through exposure.
- **The Unknowable Condition.** The forest is never explained. No mechanic makes it legible or masterable. Configuring the bus changes *how* the player meets the condition, not *whether* they can defeat it.
- **Sealed In With It.** Escape is always available in principle and always costly in practice. Ridges, the Storm, fuel economy, and disturbance all pressure toward the exit.

## Key Decisions

### Game Loop

```
GARAGE → SEED SELECTION → WORLD LOAD → DRIVE OUT →
EXPLORE / SCAVENGE → DISTURBANCE ACCUMULATES →
[STORM TRIGGERS if threshold reached] → EXIT ATTEMPT →
[EXTRACTION or DEATH] → GARAGE
```

**Lore framing**: The loop is not a game abstraction imposed on a world. It is the topology of the structure the construct is actively reshaping. The garage is the vertex: the one point all faces share. The exit corridors are edges that fold back to the vertex. Extraction and death both return the player to the garage because all paths inside the closed geometry return to the center. The player has never left. (Post-convergence: death still returns to the vertex, but extraction crosses the rim into the outside. See spec 127.) See [[The Crater]] and [[The Temporal Fracture]].

Engine states:

| State | Description |
|---|---|
| GARAGE | Player on foot in garage. Van accessible. No disturbance accumulation. |
| LOADING | World generation in progress. Seed locked. |
| DRIVING | Player in vehicle, world active. Disturbance accumulates. |
| ON_FOOT | Player outside vehicle. Disturbance accumulates. Maximum vulnerability. |
| STORM_ACTIVE | Storm spawned. Prior states continue. Escape window open. |
| EXTRACTED | Player reached exit gate. Run success. Return to garage. |
| DEAD | Player HP to zero or petrification completed. Run failure. Return to garage. |

Run success: vehicle crosses exit gate with player inside. Run failure: player HP zero, Storm catches player in open, petrification completes on foot, or engine seizure in Petrified Zone with no recovery window. Both outcomes return the player to the garage — the vertex. The difference is how much damage the circuit did on the way through. No campaign end state in v1.0 — the garage contamination arc and player exposure arc provide long-term narrative progression toward the convergence endpoint, which is not a conclusion but a phase transition: after convergence, death still returns to the vertex, but extraction crosses the rim into the outside. The game rules change. See The Temporal Fracture and spec 127.

### Player — Health

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Maximum health | 100 HP |
| Starting health (per run) | 100 HP |
| Medkit restore | 25 HP |
| Regen | None |
| Death threshold | 0 HP |

Health does not regenerate. Only restoration is medkit use. Tracked via breathing audio, screen-edge vignette (dark, not colored), and interaction speed reduction at low health. No numeric display.

### Player — Stamina

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Maximum stamina | 100 units |
| Sprint drain | 20 units/sec |
| Interact drain | 5 units/action |
| Contact escape drain | 30 units |
| Recharge (walking) | 10 units/sec |
| Recharge (crouching/stationary) | 15 units/sec |
| Recharge (inside van) | 20 units/sec |
| Minimum for sprint | 10 units |

No HUD. Read through movement-speed degradation and audible breathing. Sprint locks at <10 units.

### Player — Exposure (Cross-Run)

Persistent value tracking cumulative contact with the condition across all runs. Does not reset on death or extraction. Does not decrease. Accumulates in the player the same way garage contamination accumulates in the garage — one direction, no instrument, no remedy.

| Threshold | Symptom |
|---|---|
| 0–20 | No symptoms |
| 21–40 | Persistent cough audio, occasional sound delay (50ms) |
| 41–60 | Warmth sensation in hands (haptic/audio), smell sensitivity (audio mix) |
| 61–80 | Vision film at edges, 10% stamina-capacity reduction |
| 81–100 | `[PENDING]` — endpoint design required before implementation |

Exposure sources:
- Spore Cloud on foot: +5 per 10s of contact
- Mycelium Network on foot: +10 per contact event
- Extended Fungal Depths on foot: +2 per minute
- Deep Fungal runs (>50% run time in Fungal): +5 on extraction
- Extended on-foot time at Agitated+ disturbance: +1 per minute

No direct display. Symptoms are designed to feel ordinary — cough, warmth, slight unreliability — so players do not immediately understand what is accumulating.

### Player — Movement

| Mode | Noise Radius | Speed | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Crouch | 0m (silent) | 2 m/s | Only fully silent movement |
| Walk | 3m | 4 m/s | Standard |
| Sprint | 20m | 7 m/s | Stamina drain; noise travels mycelium |
| Fall impact | 15m | — | One-time event on hard landing |

Noise radius is the distance at which the condition registers a signal. Signal strength decreases with distance within the radius.

### Player — Flashlight

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Battery life | 5 minutes continuous; 2 minutes recharge in bus |
| Batteries found per world | 0–2 `[PENDING]` |
| Verdant beam | Normal |
| Fungal Depths beam | Scattered by haze; −40% effective range |
| Petrifold beam | High reflection off calcite surfaces |

Only on-foot tool other than throwable rocks and flare gun. No combat applications.

### Vehicle — Base Specifications

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Model | 1963 VW Type 2 (T1) 23-Window Deluxe Samba |
| Weight | ~1,100 kg |
| Engine | 50 HP, rear-mounted |
| Drive | Rear-wheel drive |
| Handling feel | Lumbering, floaty, momentum-heavy |
| Max fuel | 100 units |
| Starting fuel (per run) | 80 units |
| Max vehicle health | 100 HP |
| Destructible panels | 56 |

### Vehicle — Fuel Consumption

| Biome | Rate | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Verdant Old Growth | 1 unit/km | Baseline |
| Fungal Depths | 1.6 units/km | Spore haze affects combustion |
| Petrifold | 0.7 units/km | Engine runs lean and cold |
| Idling | 0.2 units/min | All biomes |

Petrifold's improved fuel economy is not explained by any in-world mechanic the player is told. It is noticed, not announced.

### Vehicle — Health and Damage

| Damage Source | HP Loss |
|---|---|
| Low-speed collision (<20 km/h) | 2–5 HP |
| Medium collision (20–50 km/h) | 8–15 HP |
| High-speed collision (>50 km/h) | 20–40 HP |
| Deadfall impact | 25 HP |
| Mycelium Network spore burst | 10 HP (exterior panels) |
| Storm exposure | 15 HP/sec |
| Presence contact (on exterior) | 0 HP — condition presence does not damage bus mechanically |

Panel damage distributes across the 60-panel system (56 body panels + 4 tires). Each panel tracks its own damage state. Panels at 0 HP do not fall off — they deform and remain, accumulating visual damage. Aggregate panel damage contributes to overall vehicle health. Repair kits restore 20 HP per kit, targetable at specific panel groups or the drivetrain.

### Vehicle — Electrical System

The electrical system is old and unstable. Stress events cause transient failures.

| Stress Source | Effect | Recovery |
|---|---|---|
| Hollow Tree (20m) | Instrument drift, radio static | Auto on exit from radius |
| Hollow Tree (10m) | Engine power −40%, lights flicker | Auto on exit |
| Hollow Tree (5m) | Engine near-failure, instruments dead | Auto on exit |
| Storm proximity (<50m) | Full electrical failure | Auto if Storm not caught |
| High disturbance (Agitated+) | Intermittent instrument failure | Auto; frequency increases |

Electrical failure does not strand the bus unless combined with Petrified Zone seizure. Engine will restart after exit from stress radius.

### Vehicle — Dashboard Instruments

All vehicle-state feedback is diegetic. No HUD overlays.

| Instrument | Normal | Degraded (Agitated) | Failed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fuel gauge | Accurate | ±10% error | Stuck at last reading |
| Speedometer | Accurate | Minor drift | Inaccurate |
| Tachometer | Accurate | Jittery | Inaccurate |
| Gear indicator | Accurate | Delayed | Dark |
| Battery gauge | Stable | Flickering | Dark |

At Agitated, instruments become unreliable enough that the player must estimate fuel and speed from engine audio and road feel.

### Vehicle — The Bus as Force

At speed, the bus makes contact with whatever is standing in the road. What is in the road is not an entity with a health pool — it is the condition at a local concentration, present and not moving. Contact at speed disperses that concentration. It does not kill anything.

| Speed at Contact | Bus Damage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| <10 km/h | 0 | Contact registered, no panel damage |
| 10–30 km/h | 2–8 HP (exterior panels) | Low-speed brush |
| 30–60 km/h | 10–20 HP (exterior panels) | Standard impact |
| >60 km/h | 25–40 HP (exterior panels) | High-speed, significant panel damage |

Contact at higher disturbance produces denser concentrations and proportionally greater panel damage.

### Resources

| Item | Effect | Collection | Disturbance Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fuel canister | +25 fuel | Drive-by or on foot | +3 |
| Repair kit | +20 vehicle HP (targeted) | Drive-by or on foot | +4 |
| Medkit | +25 player HP | On foot only (stop required) | +5 |
| Flare gun | Distraction tool, single use | On foot only (stop required) | +3 to find |
| Flashlight battery | +5 min flashlight | On foot only | +3 |
| Rock | Throwable distraction | Passive (always available) | +0.5/throw |

Spawn rates: fuel canister common (gas stations, ranger stations, roadsides); repair kit common (ranger stations, trailers, cargo containers); medkit uncommon (ranger stations, first aid cabinets); flare gun rare (research trailers, one per world max); flashlight battery uncommon (structures, vehicle gloveboxes).

Carry limits (field): fuel canister ×2, repair kit ×2, medkit ×2, flare gun ×1, flashlight battery ×3, rock unlimited. Garage storage: unlimited for fuel/repair/battery; medkit cabinet holds 3; flare gun not storable (found in field only); rocks N/A.

Fuel canisters and repair kits can be collected from inside a moving vehicle at speeds up to 20 km/h. Player must pass within 2m. Collection automatic on proximity — primary method for minimizing on-foot time. On-foot items require a 3-second interact animation; player is stationary and vulnerable during this time.

### Flare Gun Mechanics

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Uses | 1 (single shot, found item) |
| Carry limit | 1 at a time |
| Draw radius | 80m |
| Burn duration | 45 seconds |
| Effect | Condition attention redirects toward flare location for burn duration |
| Post-burn | Attention dissipates from flare location over ~10 seconds |
| Disturbance cost (fire) | +6 |

Not a weapon. Creates a temporary attention sink — redirecting the condition's local concentration toward heat and light, useful for clearing a path to the bus or to an exit, never for confrontation.

### Garage Systems

Single-room structure. Player explores on foot. Bus occupies center bay. All interaction points peripheral.

| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| Repair workbench | Spend repair kits on panel groups, drivetrain, or installed components |
| Fitting station | Install, remove, inspect vehicle components `[PENDING spec 027]` |
| First-aid cabinet | Use or store medkits (max 3) |
| Wall map | Seed selection. Displays biome zones for selected seeds |
| Inventory shelf | Stored items: batteries, spare repair kits, uninstalled components |
| Run notebook | Passive display near workbench. Per-run statistics, death/extraction counts, per-biome time. Read-only |
| Van (exterior) | Inspect panel damage and installed component condition visually |
| Van (interior) | Glovebox (battery storage), radio controls, footwell loading. Enter to begin run |

Repair workbench allocates repair kits to: exterior panels (front/rear/left/right/roof), mechanical systems (engine, drivetrain), electrical systems (instruments, headlights, radio). Each kit restores 20 HP, distributed across targeted system. Multiple kits can be applied to same system.

### Garage Contamination Progression

Persistent, cross-run. Does not decrease.

| Threshold | Visual Change | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Clean | Starting state |
| 10 | Moss in northwest corner | First visible sign |
| 25 | Fungal bloom on floor near vehicle | Matches Fungal Depths wheel well bloom |
| 40 | Mineral deposit at base of treeline wall | Matches Petrifold calcite |
| 60 | Mycelium thread on first-aid cabinet hinge | Recognizable to attentive players |
| 80 | Amber light visible through window at night | The forest is producing its signal inside the safe space |
| 100 | `[PENDING]` — epic event | |

Accumulates by: run completed (extraction) +3; deep Fungal run +5; Petrifold entry +3; death +2; Mycelium contact +1 per contact (cumulative).

### The Window

The single garage window faces the treeline. Always present. Cannot be boarded or obscured. Provides ambient exterior audio (forest at reduced volume) and, at high contamination, Amber Bleed is visible through it from inside the garage. First indication that the process has entered the safe space in a meaningful way.

### On-Foot Systems

All on-foot interactions have a 3-second animation with no skip. Player is stationary and vulnerable. Cancellable-by-movement: resource collection, structure entry.

**Vehicle entry/exit**: ~1.5-second camera interpolation. Player is vulnerable throughout — neither fully inside nor fully outside; the condition does not distinguish this transition from full on-foot exposure. Intentional.

**On-foot noise** (additive with bus noise when player is outside and bus is idling nearby):

| Action | Radius | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| Crouch | 0m | — |
| Walking | 3m | Continuous |
| Sprinting | 20m | Continuous |
| Fall impact | 15m | 3s |
| Interaction (pickup) | 5m | 1s |
| Grab escape | 20m | 2s |

### UI Philosophy — No HUD

No health bar. No fuel %. No disturbance meter. No minimap. No objective markers.

Information available through:
- Dashboard instruments (vehicle state)
- Van audio (engine, damage, electrical)
- Environmental audio (disturbance state, condition presence)
- Visual environment (biome, weather, anomaly signatures)
- The player's body (breathing, movement capability)

**Permitted UI surfaces**:

| Surface | Context | Content |
|---|---|---|
| Garage wall map | Garage only, on foot | Seed selection, biome zones |
| Inventory screen | Garage or stopped bus | Current inventory, management |
| Dashboard instruments | Always (in van) | Fuel, speed, RPM, gear, battery |
| Interaction prompts | Proximity-triggered | Minimal single verb (TAKE/OPEN/ENTER) |

Prompts appear only within interaction range. No waypoints, quest markers, objective text.

**Death screen**: hard cut to black; single audio event (silence, or forest transmission). No in-moment stats. Stats available next garage return via run notebook.
**Extraction screen**: exit gate closes behind bus; wind-chime resonance fading. Cut to garage with bus in bay. No score screen.

### Save & Persistence

**Persistent**: vehicle HP, per-panel damage states, vehicle configuration (installed components + damage), fuel level, inventory contents, player gear (once equipped, permanent), total runs, total extractions, total deaths, biome preference (last selected), per-biome statistics (time, runs entered, extractions from), garage contamination level (0–100, never decreases), player exposure level (0–100, never decreases).

**Does not persist**: world layout (regenerated per seed per run), condition concentration zones (influenced by seed but not fixed), resource positions (randomized within structure/road rules each run), anomaly activation states (reset each run), disturbance meter (resets to 0 each run), player health mid-run (resets to persistent value on garage return).

**Save trigger**: auto-save fires exactly once per run cycle on garage return after extraction or death. No manual save. No mid-run save. Application closed mid-run = treated as death on next launch.

### Progression — Tradeoff-First Framework

The original prohibition on numerical upgrades (pre-2.19.0 constitution) is replaced by a tradeoff-first framework. Numerical progression is permitted iff all three:

1. **Diegetically grounded.** Change is a physical thing on the bus or worn by the player. No abstract stat increases.
2. **Genuine tradeoff.** No component is a pure upgrade. Every gain carries a corresponding cost.
3. **Bounded.** Components have fixed stats. No escalating tiers, upgrade trees, or compounding bonuses.

The condition cannot be overcome. A fully-configured bus with optimal tradeoffs is still subject to the same disturbance rules, Storm, and condition. Configuration is playstyle expression, not power escalation.

**Valid progression types**:

| Type | Description | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Informational | Player gains knowledge, not statistics | Wall map annotations, notebook records |
| Narrative | Progression against the player | Garage contamination, player exposure |
| Physical (tradeoff) | Diegetic, bounded, with genuine cost | Vehicle components, worn gear |

**Prohibited**: abstract stat upgrades (not diegetically grounded); pure upgrades (gain without cost); escalating tiers (not bounded); fuel capacity upgrades (no physical basis in van configuration); HP upgrades without physical component.

### Vehicle Configuration System (§16a)

The bus can be fitted with physical components altering behavior. All components durable, degrade with use, require workbench repair. Installed components persist across runs. Destroyed beyond repair = gone permanently. Full specification (stat tables, crafting rules, workbench UI, epic unlocks) deferred to spec 027.

**Categories**: body panels, bumpers, lights, accessories, spoilers, roll cages, other fittings.

**Tradeoff examples** (illustrative, not final):

| Component | Benefit | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Heavy steel bumper | +impact force, −bus damage on road contact | +noise on impact, −top speed |
| Rear stabilizer wing | +stability at speed | +wind noise (disturbance) |
| Full roll cage | +van HP pool | +rattle audio signature (disturbance) |
| Roof-mounted aux lights | +forward visibility range | +electrical draw, +disturbance when active |
| Reinforced door skins | +panel HP (doors) | +weight, −acceleration |
| External fuel mount | +fuel carry capacity | +fire risk on collision, +noise on rough terrain |

No component combination produces a net advantage. Tradeoffs cumulative.

**Degradation**: components degrade independently from 60-panel body. Degraded components retain tradeoff *costs* while losing *benefits*. Damaged roll cage still rattles but no longer contributes full HP. Repair at workbench targeting the component directly.

**Persistence**:

| State | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Installed, undamaged | Persists across runs, full effect active |
| Installed, degraded | Persists, reduced benefit, full cost |
| Installed, destroyed | Removed permanently. Cannot be recovered |
| Uninstalled (storage) | Persists in garage inventory |

**Acquisition**: `[PENDING]` — three channels proposed: scavenged (found in structures, road debris, wrecked vehicles), crafted (crafting TBD), unlocked via epics (epic system TBD). Dedicated spec required.

### Player Gear (§16b)

Player can find and equip gear (clothing, protective layers). Once equipped, permanent. Player does not manage between runs.

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Acquisition | `[PENDING]` |
| Equip behavior | Permanent on first equip. Cannot be removed |
| Mechanical effects | `[PENDING]` — exposure resistance, stamina modifiers |
| Current scope | Cosmetic only |

Intent: keep player's attention on the van, not on their character. Gear is a visible record of what the player has found, not a system to manage.

### Camera & Controls

**In-vehicle**: first-person, locked to driver seat. FOV 75° default. Player can look left/right/mirrors. Full 360° head turn at low speed. Dashboard occupies lower quarter, always visible, readable at a glance. No UI overlay on dashboard.

**On-foot**: standard first-person. FOV 80° default. No weapon viewmodel (flashlight only when active).

**Vehicle entry/exit**: 1.5-second interpolation, not skippable. Physical animation, not cut.

### Out of Scope for v1.0

- Additional biomes (architecture supports expansion)
- Multiplayer (not in scope or architecture)
- New vehicle types (Samba is the only vehicle)
- Voiced narrative (Gary TTS system is audio spec only)
- Garage narrative events (contamination epic events at 80 and 100 `[PENDING]`)
- Environmental presence system (replaces Hollow AI — spec required)
- Player/bus convergence endpoint (Exposure 81–100 and garage endpoint `[PENDING]`)
- Endpoint visual and mechanical design (World Bible direction set; implementation open)

### Accessibility Considerations (to resolve pre-ship)

- **No HUD**: players relying on visual clarity for HP/resource state have no fallback. Consider optional accessibility mode with minimal diegetically-consistent overlays (e.g. faint gauge texture rendered as part of the dashboard, not a screen overlay).
- **Audio-dependent systems** (The Silence, presence audio, disturbance shifts, radio degradation): deaf/HoH players need visual equivalents. Suggestions: subtle screen-edge coloration for disturbance state; visual indicator for Silence zone entry; captioning for radio.
- **Low-visibility environments** (night Petrifold + The Silence): players with visual impairments face compounded difficulty. Consider optional navigation audio (subtle spatial tone for exit gate direction).

Solutions must maintain the horror register.

## How It Appears In-Game

The player learns the loop empirically. The first run is likely lost — not punitively, but because the mechanics take time to internalize. A player who survives long enough learns that the loop is not theirs. The forest was running this cycle before the first road was cut.

## Related

- [[The Crater]] — the origin event; the higher-dimensional geometry that makes the loop topological
- [[The Temporal Fracture]] — extraction as circuit completion; the loop is the shape of the space
- [[World Model]] — the world the mechanics operate within
- [[Biomes]] — fuel, weather, and audio regimes per biome
- [[Disturbance System]] — the tension mechanic these costs feed
- [[Anomalies]] — the hazards in the world
- [[Controls]] — the input layer
- [[Tone and Horror]] — the tonal register mechanics serve
- [[Vehicle — Samba]] — implementation of the vehicle specs
- [[Vehicle — Destruction]] — implementation of panel damage
- [[Vehicle — Dashboard]] — the diegetic instrument implementation
- [[Ephemerality Thread]] — the run-reset rule
- [[The Player Causes the Storm]] — endgame consequence
- [[Constitution]] — Article II (Car Is Core), Article IV Rules 6–8 (ephemeral worlds + tradeoff progression)

Spec 156 — CI Tooling Gotchas

Two CI pitfalls discovered during spec 156 PR CI debugging: the make bump targets misparse three-component semver, and the Component SemVer CI check fails on project-config even though the pre-commit hook passes locally.

## Discovery 1 — `make bump-patch` and `make bump-minor` Misparse Versions Like 0.17.12

**Context**: After changing game-affecting files (samba_bus.gd, panel_definitions.gd, etc.) in spec 156, CI's Version Bump Check required a game version bump from 0.17.12. Running `make bump-patch` or `make bump-minor` was the prescribed remedy per the CI error message.

**Discovery**: Both `make bump-patch` and `make bump-minor` misparse semver strings with patch versions ≥10 (like 0.17.12). They output "bump version 0.17.1 -> 0.17.2" instead of correctly reading 0.17.12, then fail with `Error 16` ("No tag found to do an incremental changelog"). This means any version above 0.x.y where y ≥ 10 cannot be bumped via the make targets.

**Workaround**: Manually edit the version string in `src/project.godot` (`config/version="0.x.y"`) to the desired value. CI will sync `export_presets.cfg` automatically on merge. The game-version-check CI gate (`make game-version-check`) validates that the new version is valid SemVer.

**Root cause**: Likely in the bump script's version parsing — it interprets `0.17.12` as the first two components (`0.17`) plus the beginning of the third (`1`), treating the version as `0.17.1`.

## Discovery 2 — Component SemVer Passes Pre-Commit but Fails CI for project-config

**Context**: The pre-commit hook's auto-bump logic runs on staged files and commits the updated `component_versions.json`. But when a commit only touches `src/project.godot` (version bump), the pre-commit hook says "Component SemVer check passed" without auto-bumping the `project-config` component version. CI then compares the branch's `component_versions.json` against the base branch baseline and fails because `project-config` is unchanged.

**Discovery**: The pre-commit hook's auto-bump only triggers when it detects first-party component files that are out of date relative to git's index. When `project.godot` is changed in isolation (not alongside other bus/panel changes), the hook treats the project-config component as "in sync" because the file was just staged. But CI compares against the base branch's `component_versions.json` — which has the old project-config version — so the check fails.

**Workaround**: After bumping `project.godot`, manually bump `project-config`'s version in `src/component_versions.json` before pushing. Or combine the project.godot change with another component change so the auto-bump fires.

**Implication**: The pre-commit hook's Component SemVer check is a fast local gate, but it is NOT equivalent to the CI Component SemVer check. CI uses a baseline comparison (base branch vs PR branch) that is stricter. Relying solely on the pre-commit hook for semver can lead to CI failures.

## References

- src/project.godot — game version config
- src/component_versions.json — component version tracking
- Makefile — bump-patch, bump-minor targets (version parsing bug)
- scripts/hooks/pre-commit — auto-bump logic (project-config not always bumped)

Decision Log

The chronological record of significant design and engineering decisions across Old Growth's development. Superseded decisions are retained with rationale. Sourced from Appendix C of the constitution and from decisions captured during authoring.

<!-- Populated in Phase 6. -->

## Entries

Significant decisions across Old Growth's development. Sourced from constitution amendments (the version-change log in the constitution header), Appendix C (superseded design decisions), and significant per-spec decisions.

### Constitutional amendments (from [[Constitution]] sync impact reports)

- **v2.21.0 (2026-04-21)** — Added Article XIV — The Vault. Establishes `docs/vault/` as canonical documentation surface.
- **v2.20.0 (2026-04-20)** — Added explicit game version bump obligation (Article III Rule 15) for `src/**` or `rust/**` changes merging to `main`.
- **v2.19.0 (2026-04-19)** — Replaced Article IV Rule 8's hard prohibition on numerical upgrades with a tradeoff-first progression framework. Numerical progression permitted when diegetically grounded, a genuine tradeoff, and bounded. Vehicle configuration + player gear added to persistent data list.
- **v2.13.0** (earlier) — Major revision (content not recorded in the currently-visible SYNC IMPACT REPORT)
- **Pre-2.19.0 history** — See [[Constitution]] version-change log (lines 1–180) for the full history

### Approved-stack decisions (from [[Tech Stack Review]])

- **Godot 4.6+ over Unity/Unreal/Bevy** — Article III Rule 2 (Godot Lock)
- **Jolt physics (native) over Godot Physics** — more stable vehicle sim
- **GEVP over VehicleBody3D / custom** — raycast-based simcade controller
- **Terrain3D over HTerrain / custom** — GPU clipmap, foliage instancer
- **gdext / Rust over C# / pure GDScript** — Article III Rule 17; performance-critical logic in rust-core
- **Native Godot audio over Sound Manager / FMOD / Wwise** — sufficient for the 7-bus architecture

### Rejected alternatives (Appendix C — loaded via constitution-reference skill)

Full list of rejected design decisions lives in constitution Appendix C. Access via the `constitution-reference` OpenCode skill. Examples:
- Rejection of gradual enemy introduction (anomalies are structural, not scaling)
- Rejection of multi-vehicle designs (Article II — the Samba is the only vehicle)
- Rejection of non-ephemeral worlds (Article IV Rule 6)

### Spec-level significant decisions

- **Spec 067 (Phased Rust migration)** — migration of procedural generation into rust-core for determinism + performance
- **Spec 070 (Biome blending Rust)** — biome blend logic fully moved to Rust; 14 constants promoted to `@export`; `--auto-new-game` CLI added; `veg_counts.json` baseline established
- **Spec 078 (Hardcoded values remediation)** — promoted ~150 Class A values to `@export`; introduced 3 Config Resources (BiomeConfig, DisturbanceConfig, AudioBusConfig); VarDictionary bridge migration
- **Spec 079 (Obsidian vault)** — this spec; added Article XIV

### Governance-level decisions

- **Branch-only workflow** — direct commits to `main` prohibited (Governance / Commit Strategy Rule 6+8)
- **No `git stash`** — multi-agent concurrency (Governance Rule 7)
- **Submodule two-repo workflow** — audio submodule PRs land first; parent repo updates the pointer
- **Component SemVer** — Article III Rule 15; see [[Component SemVer Policy]]

Storm

The Storm is the endgame event: a directional wall that spawns from the ridgeline opposite the nearest exit and advances toward the player when disturbance reaches its Finishing threshold. It is not a difficulty spike, not a timer, and not weather — it is the active terraforming of the construct through physical space, momentarily unfiltered (see [[The Crater]], [[The Temporal Fracture]]).

The construct is still reshaping this space. Normally the temporal fracture diffuses this process into background distortion. When disturbance destabilizes the field past the threshold, the fracture loses coherence and the raw transformation becomes perceptible — a wall of displacement energy advancing from the crater rim. The Storm is indifferent because it is not a response to the player — it is a process that has been running since the construct entered this space, briefly made visible. The storm that kills you is the storm that is still reshaping this place.

The run ends when the player either extracts (`RunPhase.EXTRACTED`) or dies (`RunPhase.DEAD`). Both outcomes return the player to the garage — the vertex. (Post-convergence: death still returns to the vertex, but extraction crosses the rim into the outside. See spec 127.) Extraction is completing a circuit along an edge of the higher-dimensional geometry. Death is completing a circuit through the ongoing displacement. The destination is the same; the cost is different. See [[The Player Causes the Storm]] for the full ludonarrative argument.

## Trigger and State

The Storm is triggered by [[Autoloads — Disturbance]] when `level >= 85` (the Finishing threshold, tunable via `disturbance_config.tres`). At that point:

1. `Autoloads — Disturbance` emits `threshold_changed("storm")` on its own autoload signal, and emits `disturbance_storm_activated(origin, direction)` via `Events.disturbance_storm_activated` for cross-system notification
2. `Autoloads — GameState` transitions `run_phase` to `RunPhase.STORM_ACTIVE`
3. Downstream storm systems begin spawning the visual wall and audio arc

The world's temporal configuration closes; the garage — the vertex — receives the player back. Only the garage persists because it is the one point all faces of the geometry agree on (see [[Ephemerality Thread]]).

## Visual System (⏳ Not yet authored)

The Storm spawns as a directional wall on the ridgeline opposite the nearest exit and advances toward the player. The direction decision is documented in [[Governance/Tech Stack Review]] §41. The visual wall is a Godot particle / shader system — not yet assigned to a dedicated script.

Key visual design constraints:
- The storm must read at driving speed from the first-person interior camera
- It must feel *indifferent* — not targeted. See [[Design/Tone and Horror]] and [[Design/Horror Register]]
- Visibility collapses to <10m inside the storm; on-foot cold exposure is −5 HP/sec in Blizzard conditions

## Audio System (⏳ Spec 107 — waiting)

[[107 Storm Audio System]] defines the 4-phase audio arc:

| Phase | Condition | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Approach** | Storm spawned, player at distance | Subsonic pressure build, biome ambient collapse |
| **Active** | Storm wall advancing | Full roar; Horror bus at max |
| **Proximity** | Player near storm edge | Disorientation; radio dies entirely |
| **Caught** | Player inside storm | Maximum; extraction pressure absolute |

Post-extraction: a 3-second silence beat as the player passes through the geometry's edge and arrives back at the vertex. For three seconds, time is coherent — all temporal layers agree. Then the next run begins, and the player enters another face of the geometry.

Prerequisite: [[111 Audio Bus Architecture]] must ship first (adds the Horror bus the storm audio routes through).

## Relationship to Disturbance

The Storm is the visible form of disturbance at its maximum. The disturbance meter is hidden — the player never sees a number. The Storm is what the meter looks like when it arrives at a conclusion about the player. It is not a punishment. The forest is not angry. The player is *the largest unfinished input in the watershed.*

See [[The Disturbance Thread]] for the full mechanic thread and [[The Player Causes the Storm]] for the ludonarrative framing.

## Related

- [[The Crater]] — the origin event; the Storm spawns from the crater rim
- [[The Temporal Fracture]] — the Storm as the ongoing insertion momentarily unfiltered
- [[Autoloads — Disturbance]] — the threshold arithmetic that triggers the Storm (level >= 85)
- [[Autoloads — GameState]] — run_phase transitions (STORM_ACTIVE → EXTRACTED / DEAD)
- [[Audio — World Audio]] — the four-state disturbance audio arc that precedes the Storm
- [[107 Storm Audio System]] — the Storm's 4-phase audio spec (⏳ waiting on spec 111)
- [[Systems/World — Procedural Generation]] — Storm direction uses exit point positions computed during generation
- [[Design/Tone and Horror]] — the horror register the Storm must maintain (indifference, not targeting)
- [[The Player Causes the Storm]] — the full ludonarrative thread
- [[The Disturbance Thread]] — the mechanic that builds to the Storm
- [[020 Disturbance Storm]] — original spec that implemented the disturbance → Storm mechanic

Tools — Agent Skills & MCP

The skill system and the MCP (Model Context Protocol) server set form the two extension surfaces that turn a generic agent into an Old Growth agent. Skills inject domain instructions into the conversation context; MCP servers extend the tool surface with external capabilities. This note inventories both, documents the invocation pattern, and maps which agents consume which surfaces. It complements [[Tools — mcpvault]], which describes the vault MCP server in depth.

## The Two Surfaces, Compared

Skills are bodies of instructions loaded into the conversation context on demand. They contain workflows, decision matrices, and references to bundled scripts. They do not add new tools — they teach the agent how to use existing tools and external systems correctly. Skills live under `.opencode/skills/` and are loaded via the `skill` tool or as the `load_skills` parameter on the `task` tool.

MCP servers are processes (local or remote) that expose tools, resources, and prompts to the agent over the Model Context Protocol. They add new tool calls — for example, `gdai-mcp-server` exposes `play_scene`, `get_running_scene_screenshot`, `simulate_input`, and other Godot runtime operations as agent-callable tools. MCP servers are configured in `opencode.json` (project-local) and `.concourse.json` (Concourse repo-profile hook).

The two surfaces compose: a skill (e.g. `observer-qa`) tells the agent the correct workflow for visual QA; an MCP server (e.g. `gdai-mcp-server`) provides the tools that workflow invokes.

## Skill Inventory

Five skills ship in `.opencode/skills/`. Each is a directory containing a `SKILL.md` file with frontmatter (description, triggers) and a body of instructions; some bundle additional scripts or reference files.

| Skill | Directory | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `observer-qa` | `.opencode/skills/SKILL.md` (root) | MCP-first visual QA pipeline. Documents the GDAI MCP screenshot-and-analyse workflow as primary, the Observer CLI as secondary for sequence captures and CI gates, the agent trigger matrix, and the decision matrix that maps `(quality, recommendation)` pairs to ship/block actions. Loaded when working on generation code, world preview, or visual artefacts. |
| `audio-assets` | `.opencode/skills/audio-assets/SKILL.md` | TTS generation tooling, audio submodule workflow, naming conventions, and provenance requirements for Old Growth radio and ambient weather content. Loaded when authoring radio clips, KTLK Gary dialogue, weather ambient SFX, or station music. |
| `introspection` | `.opencode/skills/introspection/SKILL.md` | Vault knowledge-graph audit. Documents the three-phase pipeline (mechanical via `scripts/ci/vault_audit.py`, auto-fix via `--apply`, semantic drift via the `vault-audit-semantic` agent) and the rolling `vault/audit` PR convention. Loaded when running a vault health check, interpreting audit output, or drafting correction PRs. |
| `spec-management` | `.opencode/skills/spec-management/SKILL.md` | Spec creation and repositioning in the numbered sequence. Covers the `.specify/scripts/bash/` tooling, the NNN-Title naming convention, and the directory structure under `docs/vault/Specs/NNN Title/`. Loaded when creating, renumbering, or splitting specs. |
| `blog-posts` | `.opencode/skills/blog-posts/SKILL.md` | Jekyll devlog post authoring for the GitHub Pages site. Covers the time-release scheduling mechanism (`future: false` in frontmatter), the post frontmatter contract, and the deploy-site workflow. Loaded when drafting or scheduling a blog post. |

No skill currently embeds an MCP server in its frontmatter. Skills reference MCP tools descriptively in their bodies (for example, `observer-qa` describes the GDAI MCP screenshot workflow), but the skill loader does not bind MCP servers automatically. Agents must have the relevant MCP server configured in `opencode.json` for the skill's instructions to be actionable.

## MCP Server Inventory

Four MCP servers are wired into the project. All are local processes spawned per session — there are no remote MCP endpoints.

| MCP Server | Type | Entry Point | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gdai-mcp-server` | local | `uv run src/addons/gdai-mcp-plugin-godot/gdai_mcp_server.py` | Godot editor and runtime access. Exposes scene control (`play_scene`, `stop_running_scene`), visual capture (`get_running_scene_screenshot`), input injection (`simulate_input`), node search (`search_nodes` with `mode="running_scene"`), and editor script execution (`execute_editor_script`). The server-side Python process talks to the Godot editor through HTTP calls against the paired GDScript plugin (`gdai_mcp_plugin.gd` + `gdai_mcp_runtime.gd`) loaded as a Godot editor plugin. Required for visual QA, runtime verification, and SC-001 baseline capture. The only MCP server in `opencode.json` without an explicit `enabled: true` flag (it relies on the OpenCode default-enabled behaviour). |
| `obsidian` (mcpvault) | local | `npx -y @bitbonsai/mcpvault@0.11.0 docs/vault/` | Vault knowledge-graph read/write. See [[Tools — mcpvault]] for the full tool surface (15 tools including `read_note`, `search_notes`, `write_note`, `append_to_note`, `update_frontmatter`, `manage_tags`, `list_vault`). Required for vault session-start reads and write-back of decisions, discoveries, and session logs. |
| `blender` | local | `uv run --project ~/Workbench/Repositories/blender-mcp blender-mcp` | Blender 3D pipeline automation. Used by the `tools/blender/` pipeline for mesh separation, UV unwrap, LOD generation, and GLB export. Telemetry disabled via environment variable. |
| `comfyui` | local | `comfyui-mcp-server/.venv/bin/python3 server.py --stdio` | ComfyUI workflow execution for AI texture generation. Configured with `COMFYUI_URL=http://localhost:8000`, an output root under the user's ComfyUI install, and a project-local workflow directory at `tools/comfyui/workflows/`. Used by the texture-generation pipeline that turns Blender renders into PBR textures via SDXL img2img and RealESRGAN upscaling. |

The `.concourse.json` file enables `gdai-mcp-server` and the `gdscript` LSP at the Concourse repo-profile level, so any session opened by Concourse against this repo automatically gets Godot runtime access. The full MCP set in `opencode.json` is additive and used by direct OpenCode sessions.

## Invocation Patterns

Skills are loaded one of two ways: directly via the `skill(name="...")` tool, which injects the skill content into the current conversation; or as the `load_skills` parameter on a `task(...)` delegation, which injects the skill into the spawned subagent's context. The `load_skills` parameter is required on every `task` call — pass an empty list (`load_skills=[]`) when no skill applies.

MCP servers are auto-started by OpenCode at session creation based on `opencode.json` and `.concourse.json`. Their tools become available as namespaced calls (for example, `mcp.gdai-mcp-server.play_scene`). Agents do not invoke MCP servers explicitly; they call the exposed tools directly once a session is live.

The two surfaces combine in delegation. A typical generation-code task delegates to a subagent with `load_skills=["observer-qa"]`, expecting that subagent to follow the visual QA workflow using the `gdai-mcp-server` MCP tools. The skill provides the protocol; the MCP provides the capability.

## Skill ↔ MCP ↔ Agent Coupling

The intended runtime coupling is documented below. No code currently enforces it — the bindings are conventional, not configured.

| Skill | Primary MCP | Secondary Tools | Typical Agent |
|---|---|---|---|
| `observer-qa` | `gdai-mcp-server` | `tools/observer/` CLI for sequence captures and CI gates | Sisyphus (orchestrator); subagents working on generation code |
| `audio-assets` | none (filesystem only) | `tools/tts/` scripts, `make tts-*` targets, `make radio-*` targets | Sisyphus-Junior delegated for content tasks |
| `introspection` | `obsidian` (mcpvault) | `scripts/ci/vault_audit.py`, opencode `vault-audit-semantic` agent | Sisyphus + dedicated `vault-audit-semantic` subagent |
| `spec-management` | `obsidian` (mcpvault) | `.specify/scripts/bash/` shell tooling | Sisyphus or human via slash commands |
| `blog-posts` | `obsidian` (mcpvault) | Jekyll site under `site/`, `make site-*` targets | Sisyphus or GTM persona |

The [[Tools — Development Workbench]] note carries the full layer diagram showing how agents, skills, and MCP servers stack on top of the persona runtime, the vault, the spec system, and the CI/CD layer.

## GDAI MCP Plugin — Two-Process Architecture

The `gdai-mcp-server` MCP is unusual: it is not a single process but a paired system. The Python MCP server at `src/addons/gdai-mcp-plugin-godot/gdai_mcp_server.py` is the agent-facing surface; it speaks MCP to OpenCode. The GDScript plugin (`gdai_mcp_plugin.gd` and `gdai_mcp_runtime.gd`) is loaded by the Godot editor as an `EditorPlugin` and stands up an HTTP server inside the Godot process that exposes the actual runtime hooks (scene control, screenshot capture, input simulation). The Python MCP server reaches the editor by issuing HTTP requests via `httpx` against `http://localhost:3571` (the port is overridable via the `GDAI_MCP_SERVER_PORT` environment variable). The plugin must be installed and enabled in the Godot editor for the MCP server's tools to do anything — an MCP server with no editor on the other end returns connection errors. The plugin lives in `src/addons/`, is vendored (not edited), and is excluded from first-party linting and formatting.

## Limitations

The MCP-first model has known constraints documented in the `observer-qa` skill and AGENTS.md:

- **Editor script context** — `execute_editor_script` runs in the editor process, not the running game. It cannot call autoload signals or access running scene nodes via `Engine.get_main_loop()` while the game is playing.
- **Log buffer truncation** — `get_godot_errors(num_lines=200)` returns a rolling tail. Mid-generation log lines are often lost. Use `user://logs/` file writes for durable diagnostics (the `veg_counts.json` and `generation_*.json` files follow this pattern).
- **GDExtension editor instantiation** — Instantiating Rust GDExtension nodes via `ClassDB.instantiate()` in an editor script produces placeholder instances that cannot call Rust methods. Run the full game scene instead.

These limitations push agents toward `play_scene` + `simulate_input` + filesystem reads, which is the SC-001 / vegetation baseline procedure documented in AGENTS.md.

Garage Map Shows Previous Run

This note records the intentional design decision that the garage map (spec 092) displays the world from the player's previous run rather than generating or previewing the upcoming world.

## The Decision

When the player opens the garage map between runs, the map renders the road network, biome regions, and points of interest from their last completed (or abandoned) run. The upcoming world's seed has already been determined, but the map does not show it.

## The Reasoning

This decision serves the horror register in two ways.

First, it creates a false-safety trap. The player studies the map, plans a route, identifies landmarks. All of that planning is worthless because they are looking at a world that no longer exists. The forest resets between runs. The map is a memento of somewhere you can never return to.

Second, it reinforces the ephemerality and irreversibility themes that run through the game's design. The map is not a planning tool in the conventional sense — it is evidence of a previous encounter. It tells you what you survived (or didn't), not what you are about to face.

## Implementation Constraint

The garage map must read from persisted run data (the previous run's world record), not from the current GameState seed. It must not call any world generation functions. If no previous run exists (first run), the map shows an empty or fog-of-war state — not a generated world.

## References

- docs/vault/Specs/092 Garage Map and Trip Planner/092 Garage Map and Trip Planner.md
- docs/vault/Ephemerality Thread.md
- docs/vault/The Disturbance Thread.md

Spec 157 — Two Damage Paths to Tires

The tire damage system has two independent damage paths that both target tire panels. Adding spawn protection at only the catastrophic-impact level (tire_damage_driver) left the normal damage path unguarded, requiring a second grace at the collision processing level.

## Discovery — Dual Damage Paths to Tires

**Context**: When the player reported losing wheels on spawn, the initial fix added a `spawn_grace_frames` counter to `tire_damage_driver.gd` that suppressed the catastrophic tire-detachment check (`_on_bus_collision`) during the initial settling period. The fix did not prevent wheel loss.

**Discovery**: Tire panels can be destroyed through two independent code paths from a single collision event:

1. **Catastrophic path**: `samba_bus.gd` emits `Events.bus_collision`, which triggers `tire_damage_driver._on_bus_collision`. If force exceeds `catastrophic_force_threshold` (15000) within `_CATASTROPHIC_PROXIMITY` (1.5 m) of a tire, the tire is instantly DETACHED via `panel.take_damage(panel.current_health)`.

2. **Normal damage path**: `samba_bus.gd` calls `_damage_system.apply_damage_at_point(max_force, max_force_position)`, which finds the nearest 1-3 panels to the impact point and applies `damage_amount = force * FORCE_TO_DAMAGE_SCALE`. If a tire is the nearest panel (e.g., the bus lands on a wheel), it receives the full scaled damage — enough to destroy an 80 HP tire from a 16000N+ settling impact.

The first fix only suppressed path 1. The spawn-settling impact was still destroying tires through path 2.

**Resolution**: A two-tier grace approach was needed:
- Tier 1 (`samba_bus.gd`, `_settling_grace_remaining`): Suppresses `apply_damage_at_point` entirely for 90 frames after spawn stabilization ends. `Events.bus_collision` still fires (for the tire driver to track) but damage application and disturbance are skipped.
- Tier 2 (`tire_damage_driver.gd`, `_spawn_grace_remaining`): Longer 300-frame safety net that suppresses catastrophic tire detachment as a fallback if Tier 1 expires before the bus has fully settled.

The two tiers are independent and redundant — tier 1 is the primary defense, tier 2 is insurance against late bounces or edge cases.

## Implications

- Any future modification to spawn behavior or collision processing must account for both damage paths.
- A grace period at the bus level (`_process_collisions`) is the correct place to suppress all spawn-time damage, because both paths originate from the same collision processing call.
- The tire-level grace alone is insufficient for spawn protection but remains useful as a safety net against the catastrophic path specifically.

## References

- `src/scripts/bus/samba_bus.gd` — `_process_collisions` (line 224-230), `_settling_grace_remaining` (line 62)
- `src/scripts/bus/tire_damage_driver.gd` — `_on_bus_collision` (line 421-425), `_spawn_grace_remaining` (line 48)
- `src/scripts/bus/bus_damage_system.gd` — `apply_damage_at_point` (line 174-183)

Dashboard Telemetry and Model Routing — May 22 2026

This session added model routing visibility to the persona dashboard and closed a critical telemetry gap. The work spanned three layers: a new backend endpoint, dashboard card rendering, and a telemetry wiring fix in the Letta bridge. A significant discovery emerged when the dashboard surfaced GTM's 100% escalation rate.

## Work completed

### GET /health/model-routing endpoint

New JSON endpoint at runtime.py that reads the weekly JSONL telemetry files and classifies each LLM call into a routing tier using a `_MODEL_TIERS` mapping dict. Returns per-persona: total calls and cost, breakdown by tier (cheap/foundational/frontier), breakdown by model, escalation rate (foundational+frontier / total), and a color-coded status indicator (green <=10%, yellow 10-15%, red >15%). Supports `?window=daily|weekly|monthly` query parameter. The endpoint is polled by the dashboard every 10 seconds alongside the existing 15 health endpoints.

### Dashboard Model Routing card

New card rendered in the existing health dashboard at `:9100/dashboard` and `:9101/dashboard`. Shows per-persona escalation rate with status indicator, tier distribution with call counts and percentages, and per-model sub-breakdown with cost. Sits alongside the existing cost card (total spend by model and persona), routing card (inter-agent dispatch stats), API calls card (Prometheus counters), and audit log card.

### Letta bridge telemetry

Before this session, `record_llm_call()` in telemetry.py was only called from `llm.py`, which is orphaned — the runtime uses Letta for all LLM calls, not the direct dispatch in `llm.py`. This meant the weekly JSONL files at `logs/personas/{persona}/weekly/{iso-week}.jsonl` were never populated, and the new `/health/model-routing` endpoint returned empty data.

Fixed by adding a lazy import of `record_llm_call` in `letta_bridge.py:send_to_letta()`. After each successful Letta API call, the function extracts usage data (prompt tokens, completion tokens) from the response, resolves the agent model from the Letta agent config (cached in a module-level dict), estimates cost using a per-model pricing map, and calls `record_llm_call()`. The OTel span emission fails silently if the collector is unavailable — the weekly JSONL write and Prometheus counters are the primary telemetry path.

A `_resolve_agent_model()` helper queries the Letta agent's `model` field on first call for each agent_id and caches the result. An `_estimate_cost()` function maps model names to per-million-token rates (input, output) from a dict keyed by short model name.

### model tier mapping expansion

The `_MODEL_TIERS` dict in runtime.py was expanded to cover both bare model names (`openai/gpt-4o-mini`) and openrouter-prefixed variants (`openrouter/openai/gpt-4o-mini`) since Letta returns the full handle. Also added `openrouter/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4` mapping to `foundational` tier.

## Discovery: GTM on Sonnet for 12 days

When the dashboard first showed the Model Routing card, the GTM persona displayed a 100% escalation rate — every call was routed through `openrouter/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4` (foundational tier) instead of a cheap-tier model. Investigation revealed:

- The GTM Letta agent was created on 2026-05-10 with `claude-sonnet-4` as its default model
- The cheap-tier-default routing strategy was ratified in `Autonomous Company LLM Provider Selection` on 2026-05-08 — two days before the agent was created
- The routing layer that would enforce model selection (backlog item 28) was never implemented
- The dashboard that would surface escalation rates did not exist until this session
- The telemetry that would show the cost discrepancy was not wired until this session

The GTM agent's model was updated to `openrouter/openai/gpt-4o-mini` via the Letta API during this session. The 3 historic Sonnet calls remain in the weekly JSONL and will roll off as new cheap-tier calls accumulate. At $0.15/M input vs $3.00/M input, the GTM was operating at 20x the expected cost for its entire lifetime.

Root cause: the design was ratified but never enforced. Three separate gaps — no routing layer, no visibility dashboard, no telemetry — all had to exist simultaneously for the misconfiguration to persist undetected for 12 days. Closing any one of them would have caught it.

### Backlog items enriched

Items 25 (Intra-Session Persona Cost Telemetry), 28 (Cheap-Tier Routing Layer Spec), and 29 (Foundational-Escalation Tag Protocol) were enriched with concrete implementation context from this session, including file paths to modify, the `MODEL_DEFAULT` discrepancy in `llm.py`, the discovery that `llm.py` is orphaned, and the GTM-on-Sonnet lesson.

## References

- `personas/letta_bridge.py` — `send_to_letta()` now calls `record_llm_call()`, `_resolve_agent_model()`, `_estimate_cost()`
- `personas/telemetry.py` — `record_llm_call()`, `_record_weekly_summary()`

- **094 Swamp**: Disturbance "unreliability" is a display offset, not a change to the underlying meter value.
- **096 Waterways**: River ambient audio contributes +0.02/s passive disturbance within 20m.
